Chapter 1 Strain

1.16 Mathematics: matrices

In section 1.15 we showed how the displacement changes over a short step in any direction. Let us recall the result. Let \(P\) be an interior point of a body, that is, a point with some material around it in all directions, and let the displacement field be continuously differentiable, that is, let it have partial derivatives that exist and change without jumps (definition 1.90). From \(P\) we take a short step to the point \(Q\), so that \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z)\). By theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step, written for each component of the displacement separately, the three equalities (1.36) of section 1.15.7 hold. Let us write them out once more:

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P) &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z + R_{\mathrm{x}} , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{y}}(P) &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z + R_{\mathrm{y}} , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{z}}(P) &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z + R_{\mathrm{z}} . \end{aligned}\]

The remainders \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(R_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{z}}\) are negligible compared with the length of the step: each of them, divided by the length of the step \(|\overrightarrow{PQ}|\), goes to zero as the step gets shorter. More precisely, for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|R_{\mathrm{x}}| \le \eta\,|\overrightarrow{PQ}|\) for every step with \(0 < |\overrightarrow{PQ}| < \delta\), and the same for \(R_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{z}}\).

These three lines contain nine partial derivatives and the same pattern three times. Each line takes the three partial derivatives of one component of the displacement, multiplies each by the matching component of the step and adds the products. In the next section we will compute the strain of a fibre in any direction from these lines and rewrite them several times along the way. Nine partial derivatives written out again each time would hide what is going on. In chapter 2, too, we will describe with nine numbers how the parts of a body act on each other, and we will have to say how these numbers change when we turn the axes. So we need a way of writing in which the nine numbers are a single table (figure 1.312, right) and the threefold pattern is a single operation.

From history

Calculating with tables of numbers as with a single object was developed in 1858 by Arthur Cayley in a paper that, in the opinion of James Joseph Sylvester, began the reign of Algebra the Second (Algebra druga), that is, a new era in algebra (CAJORI, PDF p. 355-356). The origin of such calculating actually lies with Hamilton of section 1.5.2, but Cayley's theory is more general and does not mention Hamilton (CAJORI, PDF p. 356).

First we will define tables such as the table of nine partial derivatives of the displacement, and add them. Then we will multiply a table by a vector (figure 1.317), so that the three lines (1.36) become a single equation, and we will try this on the sheared cube and on the hanging bar. From two multiplications by two tables one after the other (figure 1.323) we will derive the multiplication of two tables. Then come the exchange of rows and columns, the splitting of a table into a part that does not change under this exchange and a part that changes its sign under it, and a table that leaves a vector unchanged and a table that undoes the multiplication by another table. In the next section the splitting will separate the stretching of the material from its turning. All of this is algebra. We assume only the school rules of arithmetic for numbers and the rules of vector arithmetic of section 1.5.3. We need no limits in this section.

1.16.1 A table of numbers

We already collected the nine partial derivatives of (1.36) at the end of section 1.15 in a table with three rows and three columns (figure 1.312, right), just as in section 1.7.2 we collected the partial derivatives of the hanging bar. A row holds a component of the displacement, a column the variable we differentiate with respect to. Now we enclose the table in square brackets:

\[\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P) & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}(P) & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}(P) \\[3mm] \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}(P) & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(P) & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z}(P) \\[3mm] \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}(P) & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}(P) & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}(P) \end{bmatrix} .\]

The first row of the table is exactly the three partial derivatives of the first line of (1.36), in the same order, the second row holds the partial derivatives of the second line and the third row those of the third. So the table holds everything the three equations say about the field at the point \(P\), apart from the remainders. Such tables get a name.

Definition 1.93 Matrix (matrika)

A matrix (matrika) of size \(m \times n\) is a table of real numbers with \(m\) rows (vrstice) and \(n\) columns (stolpci). The number in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is the entry (element) of the matrix at the position \((i, j)\). We denote matrices by bold capital letters, for example \(\mat A\), and their entries by the same letter with two indices, \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The first index gives the row, the second the column:

\[\mat A = \begin{bmatrix} A_{11} & A_{12} & \cdots & A_{1\mathrm{n}} \\ A_{21} & A_{22} & \cdots & A_{2\mathrm{n}} \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ A_{\mathrm{m}1} & A_{\mathrm{m}2} & \cdots & A_{\mathrm{mn}} \end{bmatrix} .\]

Two matrices are equal if they have the same size and agree in all entries at the same positions. A matrix with as many rows as columns, \(n \times n\), is a square matrix (kvadratna matrika) of order \(n\), and its entries \(A_{11}, A_{22}, \dots, A_{\mathrm{nn}}\) lie on the main diagonal (glavna diagonala). A matrix of size \(n \times 1\) is a column (stolpec), a matrix of size \(1 \times n\) a row (vrstica). For square matrices of order \(3\) that describe quantities in space we label the rows and columns by the letters \(x, y, z\) instead of the numbers \(1, 2, 3\). When we calculate with matrices, we write a vector \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) as the column

\[\vek v = \begin{bmatrix} v_{\mathrm{x}} \\ v_{\mathrm{y}} \\ v_{\mathrm{z}} \end{bmatrix} .\]

Source: KREYSZIG §7.1, (2) (PDF pp. 283-285), CM §2.3.1 (PDF pp. 60-61).

From history

The word matrix was introduced by Sylvester in September 1850, for a table of numbers from which certain expressions can be formed, while it is not itself such an expression (MUIR, PDF p. 582-584). We shall meet these expressions in chapter 2.

Let us first draw a general matrix, in the figure on the left. A rectangular table of elements \(A_{11}, \dots, A_{\mathrm{mn}}\) is a matrix, and square brackets enclose it as one whole. The dots \(\cdots\) and \(\vdots\) mean that we leave out the elements in between, because there would be too many to write out. The grey numbers at the top count the columns from \(1\) to \(n\), the grey numbers on the left count the rows from \(1\) to \(m\). Only \(1\), some column \(j\) and the last one \(n\) are written out, and likewise for the rows \(1\), some \(i\) and the last one \(m\). Under the table its size \(m \times n\) is written, that is the number of rows times the number of columns. Then we choose one element. The blue shaded horizontal band is row \(i\) and the blue shaded vertical band is column \(j\). The bands cross in the element \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), which is surrounded by a blue rectangle. The element lies in both bands at once, so it has both indices: the first tells the row, the second the column.

In the figure on the right is a square matrix of order \(3\) in square brackets. The nine fractions are the partial derivatives of the displacement at the point \(P\). The grey letters \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) on the left label the rows. Each row belongs to one component of the displacement, since it is in the numerator of all three fractions in the row. The grey letters \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) at the top label the columns. Each column belongs to one variable we differentiate with respect to, since it is in the denominator of all three fractions in the column. The blue element at the top right is in row \(x\) and column \(z\). Under the table is the size \(3 \times 3\).

A matrix is by definition \(m \cdot n\) numbers arranged in rows and columns, and the arrangement counts. Two matrices with the same numbers in different places are different matrices, just as the points \((3, 2, 2)\) and \((2, 3, 2)\) of section 1.5.1 are different points. The table of partial derivatives from the start of the section is a square matrix of order \(3\). Its element in row \(x\) and column \(y\) is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\) at the point \(P\) (figure 1.312, right). The element in row \(x\) and column \(z\) is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z\). The indices of an element follow each other in the same order as in the notation \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\): the first tells the component of the displacement (in the numerator), the second the variable we differentiate with respect to (in the denominator).

Why do we label the rows and columns of square matrices of order \(3\) with letters? Then the index tells the direction. The element \(A_{\mathrm{xz}}\) is in row \(x\) and column \(z\), and in the table of partial derivatives it tells how fast the component of the displacement in the direction of the axis \(x\) changes as we move in the direction of the axis \(z\). Many books number the axes and write the same element \(A_{13}\) (CM §2.3.1, PDF p. 60), as we mentioned with the unit vectors \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\), \(\vek e_3\) in section 1.5.5.

Until now we have written a vector as a triple in round brackets, \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) (figure 1.313). Let us draw it. The axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) point to the right, obliquely into the depth, and upwards. The arrow from the origin is the vector \(\vek v\). The grey dashed path reaches its tip along the axes: first by \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), then by \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and finally by \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\). The triple lists the same three numbers horizontally. When we calculate with matrices, we write it vertically, as a column. It is the same vector with the same three components, only arranged differently on paper. Two columns are equal exactly when they are equal vectors, since they must agree in the same three numbers. Why vertically, we will see below, when we multiply a matrix by a vector. Where there is no risk of confusion, we will also write columns in the text as triples in round brackets, to save space. The word column therefore has two meanings: a matrix with a single column, that is, a vector, and one column of a larger matrix. We write the first as the column \(\vek v\), the second as column \(k\) of the matrix \(\mat B\).

Matrices can have any size (figure 1.314). Let us draw a system of two equations in three unknowns \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), in which the unknowns are only multiplied by numbers and added. Its coefficients, the blue numbers, we write in the same order into the matrix of coefficients of size \(2 \times 3\): each equation is one row and each unknown one column. A system of \(m\) equations in \(n\) unknowns has in this way a matrix of coefficients of size \(m \times n\) (KREYSZIG §7.1, Example 1, PDF p. 283). The entries can also be functions (KREYSZIG §7.1, PDF p. 283), but we will need only real numbers. Square matrices of order \(3\) and columns with three entries are the most common case in this book, but not the only one. As soon as we multiply matrices we will also need rows of size \(1 \times 3\).

In the equations (1.36) the remainders are added to the products. When we write them with matrices, we will therefore add columns. Later we will also add square matrices. We add them as we add vectors, entry by entry. Figure 1.315 shows how.

Definition 1.94 Sum and multiple of matrices (vsota in večkratnik matrik)

For matrices \(\mat A\) and \(\mat B\) of the same size \(m \times n\) and a number \(c\), the sum \(\mat A + \mat B\) (vsota), the difference \(\mat A - \mat B\) (razlika) and the multiple \(c\,\mat A\) (večkratnik) are the matrices of size \(m \times n\) with the entries

\[(\mat A + \mat B)_{\mathrm{ij}} = A_{\mathrm{ij}} + B_{\mathrm{ij}} , \qquad (\mat A - \mat B)_{\mathrm{ij}} = A_{\mathrm{ij}} - B_{\mathrm{ij}} , \qquad (c\,\mat A)_{\mathrm{ij}} = c\,A_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]

The zero matrix (ničelna matrika) \(\mat 0\) has all entries equal to zero.

Source: KREYSZIG §7.1 (PDF p. 286), CM (2.3.2) (PDF p. 61).

The notation \((\mat A + \mat B)_{\mathrm{ij}}\) means the entry of the matrix \(\mat A + \mat B\) at the position \((i, j)\). So every entry of the sum depends only on the entries at the same position of both matrices. We do not add matrices of different sizes, because some entries of one would have no partner in the other. For example

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad 2 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 8 \\ 4 & 6 \end{bmatrix} .\]

For two columns with three entries, the sum, the difference and the multiple are exactly the sum, the difference and the multiple of vectors of definition 1.14, only written vertically. Since we calculate entry by entry, the same rules hold for matrices as for vectors.

Before we write the rules, we test them on numbers (figure 1.316).

Let us draw this. Above are three given matrices of size \(2 \times 2\), with the entry at the position \((1, 2)\) in blue in each, because we will check every rule on it. Below them, in each pair, on the left is the matrix given by the left side of the rule, on the right the matrix of the right side, and under them the expressions and the computation in blue from the entries. In the first pair are the matrices \(\mat A + \mat B\) and \(\mat B + \mat A\), with the entries \(4 + 1\) and \(1 + 4\). In the second three matrices are added in two ways, \((4 + 1) + 3\) and \(4 + (1 + 3)\). The third pair shows that the zero matrix changes nothing, the fourth that the difference of a matrix with itself is the zero matrix. The fifth shows that twice a sum equals the sum of the doubles, the sixth that a multiple with a sum of numbers equals the sum of the multiples. The seventh shows that twice the triple equals the sixfold, the eighth that multiplication by \(1\) does not change the matrix. The labels \((1)\) to \((5)\) are the numbers of the rules of the lemma.

Lemma 1.95 Rules of matrix arithmetic (računska pravila za matrike)

For all matrices \(\mat A\), \(\mat B\), \(\mat C\) of the same size and all numbers \(c\), \(k\):

  1. \(\mat A + \mat B = \mat B + \mat A\),
  2. \((\mat A + \mat B) + \mat C = \mat A + (\mat B + \mat C)\),
  3. \(\mat A + \mat 0 = \mat A\) and \(\mat A - \mat A = \mat 0\),
  4. \(c\,(\mat A + \mat B) = c\,\mat A + c\,\mat B\) and \((c + k)\,\mat A = c\,\mat A + k\,\mat A\),
  5. \(c\,(k\,\mat A) = (c\,k)\,\mat A\) and \(1\,\mat A = \mat A\).
Proof

We must show that in each rule the matrices on the left and on the right are equal.

  1. Two matrices are equal if they have the same size and agree in all entries at the same positions (definition 1.93). The sum, the difference and the multiple of matrices of size \(m \times n\) are matrices of size \(m \times n\) (definition 1.94), so both sides of every rule have the same size. It remains to check each rule for the entry at an arbitrary position \((i, j)\).
  2. All operations in the rules are defined entry by entry, so the entry \((i, j)\) of each side is computed only from the entries \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), \(B_{\mathrm{ij}}\), \(C_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and from the numbers \(c\), \(k\).
  3. Rules 1 and 2. The entry \((i, j)\) of the left and the right side is \(A_{\mathrm{ij}} + B_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(B_{\mathrm{ij}} + A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), or \((A_{\mathrm{ij}} + B_{\mathrm{ij}}) + C_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{ij}} + (B_{\mathrm{ij}} + C_{\mathrm{ij}})\). In both cases the numbers are equal, because the order of adding numbers does not affect the sum and when adding three numbers it does not matter which two we add first.
  4. Rule 3. The entry \((i, j)\) of the matrix \(\mat A + \mat 0\) is \(A_{\mathrm{ij}} + 0 = A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and the entry of the matrix \(\mat A - \mat A\) is \(A_{\mathrm{ij}} - A_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\), which is the entry of the zero matrix.
  5. Rule 4. The entry \((i, j)\) of the left side is \(c\,(A_{\mathrm{ij}} + B_{\mathrm{ij}})\) or \((c + k)\,A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), that of the right side \(c\,A_{\mathrm{ij}} + c\,B_{\mathrm{ij}}\) or \(c\,A_{\mathrm{ij}} + k\,A_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The numbers are equal by the rule for multiplying a sum by a number. For the multiple in the figure this is \(2 \cdot 4 = 8\).
  6. Rule 5. The entry \((i, j)\) of the left side is \(c\,(k\,A_{\mathrm{ij}})\) or \(1 \cdot A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), that of the right side \((c\,k)\,A_{\mathrm{ij}}\) or \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The numbers are equal, because when multiplying three numbers it does not matter which two we multiply first, and because multiplying by \(1\) does not change a number.
  7. Both sides of every rule agree in all entries, so by step 1 they are equal.

Source: KREYSZIG §7.1, (3) and (4) (PDF pp. 286-287), CM §2.3.2 (PDF p. 61).

The proof is the same as the proof of lemma 1.15 on the rules of vector arithmetic, only that instead of three components we check all entries. Matrices of the same size, with their addition and multiplication by numbers, therefore meet all the requirements of a vector space (KREYSZIG §7.9, Example 1, PDF p. 337), which definition 1.16 lists. There we mentioned that tables of numbers of size \(2 \times 2\) are vectors in this sense, and the lemma confirms it for all sizes. So we may calculate with matrices just as with vectors: move the terms of a sum around, shift brackets and take numbers out as factors.

1.16.2 A matrix times a vector

Now let us write the three sums. Look at the first line of (1.36) without the remainder:

\[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z .\]

Its first factors are the first row of the matrix of partial derivatives, its second factors are the components of the step, which we write as a column. Figure 1.317 shows the same for an arbitrary matrix and its second row.

Let us draw the multiplication in parts. On the left is the matrix \(\mat A\) with nine elements \(A_{\mathrm{xx}}, \dots, A_{\mathrm{zz}}\), next to it the column \(\vek v\) with the components \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\). The sign \(=\) separates the factors from the result. The result is a column with three elements, each written as a sum of three products. Let us choose the second element of the result, the element \(y\). The blue shaded element is therefore the middle one. We compute it from row \(y\) of the matrix, which is shaded in the same colour, and from the column \(\vek v\). The blue horizontal arrow under the row shows that we go along the row from left to right. The blue vertical arrow next to the column shows that we go at the same time along the column from top to bottom. So \(A_{\mathrm{yx}}\) meets \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(A_{\mathrm{yy}}\) meets \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{yz}}\) meets \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\), which can also be seen in the expression for the element \(y\) of the result.

We get the sum by walking along the row and down the column at the same time, multiplying the numbers at matching positions and adding the products. The sum is written in the entry of the result. The second line of (1.36) is the same sum with the second row of the matrix and the same column, the third with the third row. This operation gets a name.

Definition 1.96 Product of a matrix and a vector (produkt matrike in vektorja)

Let \(\mat A\) be a matrix of size \(m \times n\) and \(\vek v\) a column with \(n\) entries \(v_1, \dots, v_{\mathrm{n}}\). The product (produkt) \(\mat A\vek v\) is the column with the \(m\) entries

\[\begin{aligned} (\mat A\vek v)_{\mathrm{i}} &= \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}} = A_{\mathrm{i}1}\,v_1 + A_{\mathrm{i}2}\,v_2 + \dots + A_{\mathrm{in}}\,v_{\mathrm{n}} , \\ &\qquad i = 1, \dots, m . \end{aligned} \tag{1.38}\]

The sign \(\sum\) means the sum of the terms \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\) for \(j = 1, \dots, n\), as the written-out form shows. For a square matrix of order \(3\) and a vector \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) this is

\[\mat A\vek v = \begin{bmatrix} A_{\mathrm{xx}} & A_{\mathrm{xy}} & A_{\mathrm{xz}} \\ A_{\mathrm{yx}} & A_{\mathrm{yy}} & A_{\mathrm{yz}} \\ A_{\mathrm{zx}} & A_{\mathrm{zy}} & A_{\mathrm{zz}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} v_{\mathrm{x}} \\ v_{\mathrm{y}} \\ v_{\mathrm{z}} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} A_{\mathrm{xx}}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} + A_{\mathrm{xy}}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} + A_{\mathrm{xz}}\,v_{\mathrm{z}} \\ A_{\mathrm{yx}}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} + A_{\mathrm{yy}}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} + A_{\mathrm{yz}}\,v_{\mathrm{z}} \\ A_{\mathrm{zx}}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} + A_{\mathrm{zy}}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} + A_{\mathrm{zz}}\,v_{\mathrm{z}} \end{bmatrix} .\]

Source: KREYSZIG §7.2, (1) and Example 2 (PDF pp. 289-290), CM (2.3.6) (PDF p. 63).

The sign \(\sum\), the capital Greek letter sigma, is short for a sum. The expression \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\) means that in the expression \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\) we put in turn \(1, 2, \dots, n\) for \(j\) and add the \(n\) terms we get. The index \(j\) under the sign is called the summation index (indeks seštevanja). For a square matrix of order \(3\) it runs over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), and \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{xj}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\) is \(A_{\mathrm{xx}}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} + A_{\mathrm{xy}}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} + A_{\mathrm{xz}}\,v_{\mathrm{z}}\). We will always write sums with this sign or written out, and we will never leave the sign out, as some books do (CM §2.2.5, PDF pp. 52-53).

So the entry \(i\) of the product is row \(i\) of the matrix times the column: we multiply each entry of the row by the entry of the column at the matching position and add the products. That is why we write the vector vertically. The product exists only if the matrix has as many columns as the column has entries, since every entry of the row must get its partner. The result has as many entries as the matrix has rows.

With the product, the three lines (1.36) are a single equation (figure 1.318). On the left stands the column of differences of displacements, the sign \(=\) equates it with the product of the matrix of partial derivatives and the column of the step, to which the sign \(+\) adds the column of remainders. The row shaded in blue is the first line of (1.36): the left side, the first row of the matrix, the component \(\Delta x\) and the remainder \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\). The second and third rows belong to the second and third lines of (1.36):

\[\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P) \\[1mm] u_{\mathrm{y}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{y}}(P) \\[1mm] u_{\mathrm{z}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{z}}(P) \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P) & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}(P) & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}(P) \\[3mm] \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}(P) & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(P) & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z}(P) \\[3mm] \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}(P) & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}(P) & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}(P) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \Delta x \\[1mm] \Delta y \\[1mm] \Delta z \end{bmatrix} \\ &\quad + \begin{bmatrix} R_{\mathrm{x}} \\[1mm] R_{\mathrm{y}} \\[1mm] R_{\mathrm{z}} \end{bmatrix} . \end{aligned} \tag{1.39}\]

Let us check that this really is the same. By definition 1.96 the entry \(x\) of the product is the first row of the matrix times the column of the step, which is the sum in the first line of (1.36). When by definition 1.94 we add the entry \(x\) of the column of remainders, \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\), we get the right side of the first line of (1.36). The left side is the entry \(x\) of the column on the left. The same holds for the entries \(y\) and \(z\). The column on the left is the difference of the displacement vectors \(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\), written vertically, and the column of the step is the vector \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\). Nine numbers and three sums are now one matrix and one product.

Let us try the notation first on the sheared cube of section 1.6.2. We glued a steel cube with an edge of 10 mm, that is, \(10\,000\) µm, to a table by its bottom face and pushed its top face sideways by 10 µm. The origin is at the lower front left corner \(A\), the axis \(x\) points in the direction of the push, the axis \(z\) vertically up, and we measure lengths in micrometres. The corners of the front face are, in micrometres, \(A = (0, 0, 0)\), \(B = (10\,000, 0, 0)\), \(C = (10\,000, 0, 10\,000)\) and \(D = (0, 0, 10\,000)\) (figure 1.319).

The hatched line at the bottom is the table to which the cube is glued, so the bottom edge cannot move. The axes on the left show that the axis \(x\) points to the right and the axis \(z\) up. The grey shaded square is the front face before loading. Its corners are \(A\) at the bottom left, \(B\) at the bottom right, \(C\) at the top right and \(D\) at the top left. The orange parallelogram is the same face after loading. We pushed the top edge to the right, the bottom edge stayed on the table. The shift is strongly enlarged in the figure, in reality the ratio of the shift to the height is \(0{,}001\), which we would not see. The orange dimension lines \(u\) above the top edge show how far the corners \(D\) and \(C\) moved. The dimension lines are equal, because the top edge moves as a whole, and each is \((10, 0, 0)\) µm. The three blackwhite arrows from \(A\) are the vectors of the fibres. The arrow \(AB\) lies on the bottom edge, the arrow \(AD\) on the left edge and the arrow \(AC\) on the diagonal. Each points from \(A\) towards another corner, because the vector of the fibre \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) tells where we go from \(A\) to reach \(B\).

The displacement field of the cube (figure 1.319) is

\[u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z) = 0{,}001\,z , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) = 0 , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z) = 0\]

((1.16)). We compute the partial derivatives as in section 1.7.2, treating the variables we do not differentiate with respect to as fixed numbers. The component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) changes only with \(z\), at the rate \(0{,}001\), so \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z = 0{,}001\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y = 0\). The components \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) are zero everywhere, so all their partial derivatives are zero. The matrix of partial derivatives is therefore the same at every point of the cube. We denote it by \(\mat K\):

\[\mat K = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}001 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The only nonzero entry is in row \(x\) and column \(z\). The component of the displacement in the direction of the axis \(x\) changes as we go in the direction of the axis \(z\), upward, as in the deck of cards, whose layers slide the more the higher they lie.

For the cube there are no remainders. The difference \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P) = 0{,}001\,z_{\mathrm{Q}} - 0{,}001\,z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0{,}001\,\Delta z\) is exactly the product of the partial derivative and the component of the step, because the field has no squares or products of coordinates, and the other two differences are zero. The difference of displacements of the ends of every fibre of the cube is therefore exactly \(\mat K\) times the vector of the fibre. Let us check this on the vertical edge \(AD\) with the vector \(\overrightarrow{AD} = (0, 0, 10\,000)\):

\[\mat K \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 10\,000 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 0 + 0{,}001 \cdot 10\,000 \\ 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 10\,000 \\ 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 10\,000 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

This is exactly \(\vek u(D) - \vek u(A) = (10, 0, 0) - (0, 0, 0)\): the top of the edge moves by 10 µm in the direction of the axis \(x\), the bottom does not move. We get the same for the diagonal \(AC\), \(\mat K\,\overrightarrow{AC} = \mat K\,(10\,000, 0, 10\,000) = (10, 0, 0)\), and for the bottom edge, \(\mat K\,\overrightarrow{AB} = \mat K\,(10\,000, 0, 0) = (0, 0, 0)\). By (1.15) the vector of a fibre after loading is its vector before loading plus the difference of displacements of its ends. For the edge \(AD\) this is \((0, 0, 10\,000) + (10, 0, 0) = (10, 0, 10\,000)\), as in the table of section 1.6.2. So the whole deformation of the cube is stored in a single number, \(0{,}001\), in the right place of the matrix \(\mat K\).

Two properties of the product follow from the rules for numbers, and we will use them all the time.

We prove the lemma on one entry of the result (figure 1.320).

Let us first draw the upper row. The matrix \(\mat A\) of size \(m \times n\) has the row \(i\) shaded in blue. On the right stands the column \(\vek v + \vek w\) with \(n\) entries, and the result \(\mat A\,(\vek v + \vek w)\) is a column with \(m\) entries, in which the entry \(i\) is blue. The same column must be the sum of the columns \(\mat A\vek v\) (blue) and \(\mat A\vek w\) (orange), also with \(m\) entries. The middle table computes the entry \(i\), for example for \(n = 3\). Top left are the terms \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,(v_{\mathrm{j}} + w_{\mathrm{j}})\), one for each \(j = 1, 2, 3\). On the right each is expanded into a blue term with \(v_{\mathrm{j}}\) and an orange term with \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\). Both sums, blue and orange, are by definition the entry \(i\) of the column \(\mat A\vek v\) and of the column \(\mat A\vek w\). The lower table is for the multiple. Its terms \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,c\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\) are each equal to \(c\,A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\), so \(c\) stands in front of the sum.

Lemma 1.97 Linearity of the product with a matrix (linearnost produkta z matriko)

For every matrix \(\mat A\) of size \(m \times n\), all columns \(\vek v\) and \(\vek w\) with \(n\) entries and every number \(c\) the first and the second equality hold:

\[\mat A\,(\vek v + \vek w) = \mat A\vek v + \mat A\vek w , \qquad \mat A\,(c\,\vek v) = c\,(\mat A\vek v) .\]
Proof

We must show that the columns on the left and on the right of each equality agree in every entry.

  1. Both sides of each equality are columns with \(m\) entries, because the product with the matrix \(\mat A\) has as many entries as \(\mat A\) has rows (definition 1.96), and the sum and the multiple of columns with \(m\) entries have \(m\) entries (definition 1.94). We compare the entry \(i\).
  2. The entry \(j\) of the column \(\vek v + \vek w\) is \(v_{\mathrm{j}} + w_{\mathrm{j}}\) (definition 1.94). By (1.38) the entry \(i\) of the left side of the first equality is therefore \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,(v_{\mathrm{j}} + w_{\mathrm{j}})\).
  3. We expand each term by the rule for multiplying a sum by a number, \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,(v_{\mathrm{j}} + w_{\mathrm{j}}) = A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}} + A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,w_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  4. A sum of \(2n\) terms does not depend on the order of adding, so we arrange the terms in two sums, \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,w_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  5. By (1.38) the first sum is the entry \(i\) of the column \(\mat A\vek v\) and the second the entry \(i\) of the column \(\mat A\vek w\). Their sum is the entry \(i\) of the column \(\mat A\vek v + \mat A\vek w\) (definition 1.94). The first equality holds.
  6. The entry \(j\) of the column \(c\,\vek v\) is \(c\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\), so by (1.38) the entry \(i\) of the left side of the second equality is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,c\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  7. In each term we change the order of the factors, \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,c\,v_{\mathrm{j}} = c\,A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\), and take the common factor \(c\) out in front of the sum by the rule for multiplying a sum by a number. We get \(c \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  8. This is the number \(c\) times the entry \(i\) of the column \(\mat A\vek v\), that is, the entry \(i\) of the column \(c\,(\mat A\vek v)\) (definition 1.94). The second equality holds.

Source: KREYSZIG §7.2, (2a) and (2d) (PDF p. 290), §7.9, (10) and (11) (PDF p. 340).

Let us first draw the left half of the figure. The hatched line at the bottom is the table, the grey square is the front face of the cube, glued to the table, and the axes in the corner show \(x\) to the right and \(z\) up. The thick line is the fibre with the vector \(\vek v\), with dots at its ends. The blue dimension line with limit ticks at the upper end is the difference of the displacements of the ends, \(\mat K\vek v\). It is drawn horizontally, because the displacement of the cube is horizontal, and next to the upper end only so that it is next to the fibre. It shows the difference between the displacements of the two ends, not the displacement of the upper point. Its length is strongly enlarged, because in reality it would be a thousand times shorter than the height of the fibre. The shorter fibre to the right of the first is parallel to it and half as long, so it has the vector \(\tfrac12\vek v\). Its blue dimension line \(\tfrac12\mat K\vek v\) is half as long as the first.

Now the right half. The hatched line and the grey square are again the table and the front face of the cube. The path has three points: \(P\), \(Q\) and \(S\). The fibre \(\vek v\) leads from \(P\) to \(Q\), the fibre \(\vek w\) from \(Q\) to \(S\) and the thinner line from \(P\) straight to \(S\) is the fibre \(\vek v + \vek w\). It is thinner because it is a shortcut, not part of the path. The first blue dimension line at \(Q\) is the difference of displacements \(\mat K\vek v\) on the first part of the path. The blue dimension line at the top is the difference of displacements \(\mat K(\vek v + \vek w)\) on the shortcut. The lower double dimension line at \(S\) puts the blue dimension line \(\mat K\vek w\) behind the grey dimension line \(\mat K\vek v\), which is a copy of the first. Together they are as long as the dimension line at the top. Here too the blue dimension lines are strongly enlarged, but in a different ratio than on the left: there the ratio of the dimension line to the fibre is \(0{,}4\), here \(0{,}5\), and in reality \(0{,}001\).

What does the lemma say about fibres? In the cube take a fibre with the vector \(\vek v\) and a fibre pointing in the same direction and half as long, with the vector \(\tfrac12\,\vek v\) (figure 1.321, left). By the second equality of the lemma, the difference of displacements of the ends of the shorter fibre is \(\mat K\,(\tfrac12\,\vek v) = \tfrac12\,\mat K\vek v\), half as large. For a fibre along the diagonal \(AC\) and half as long as it, this is \(\tfrac12\,(10, 0, 0) = (5, 0, 0)\), as we found without matrices in section 1.6.2. The first equality says that differences of displacements add up along a path (figure 1.321, right). From the point \(P\) we get to the point \(S\) directly, with the vector \(\vek v + \vek w\), or first with the vector \(\vek v\) to the point \(Q\) and then with the vector \(\vek w\) to \(S\). The difference of displacements between \(P\) and \(S\) is \(\mat K\,(\vek v + \vek w)\), the sum of the differences over the two parts of the path is \(\mat K\vek v + \mat K\vek w\). The lemma says they are equal. And so they must be, since \(\vek u(S) - \vek u(P) = \big(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\big) + \big(\vek u(S) - \vek u(Q)\big)\), as in the splitting of a step in equation (1.22).

Multiplication by a matrix \(\mat A\) of size \(m \times n\) is a rule whose input is a column \(\vek v\) of \(n\) numbers and whose output is the column \(\mat A\vek v\) of \(m\) numbers. So it is a function in the sense of definition 1.4, with both sets being sets of columns. A function whose input is an element of some vector space and whose output is an element of the same or another vector space, and which has both properties of lemma 1.97 on the linearity of the product with a matrix, written with the addition and the multiplication by numbers of these spaces, is called a linear map (linearna preslikava) in mathematics (KREYSZIG §7.9, (10), PDF pp. 339-340). Every multiplication by a matrix is a linear map, with both spaces being spaces of columns. The converse also holds: every linear map whose input is \(n\) numbers and whose output is \(m\) numbers is the multiplication by some matrix of size \(m \times n\) (KREYSZIG §7.9, PDF pp. 340-341). So a matrix has three roles. It is a table of numbers (definition 1.93), it is an element of a vector space (lemma 1.95), and it represents a linear map (lemma 1.97).

Now the hanging bar, where the remainders are not zero. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m with a diameter of 10 mm hangs under its own weight. As in section 1.7.1 it is held in an idealized way: only the point \(O\), the centre of the top end, is fixed, and a force pulling evenly upward on the top face carries the weight of the bar. The axis \(x\) points vertically down from \(O\), the axes \(y\) and \(z\) lie horizontally. The point \(P\) lies at a depth of 5 m, 4 mm to the right of the axis of the bar, so \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 0{,}004\) m and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\). We computed the table of partial derivatives at the point \(P\) in section 1.7.2. Let us write it as a matrix and denote it by \(\mat V\), after the initial of the Slovenian word viseča, hanging:

\[\mat V = \begin{bmatrix} 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} & -4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} & 0 \\ 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} .\]

From \(P\) we draw a fibre of length \(h\) in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23)\) of section 1.7.3, whose length is \(\sqrt{1/9 + 4/9 + 4/9} = 1\) (figure 1.322 below). The vector of the fibre is \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = h\,\vek n\). By (1.39) and the second equality of lemma 1.97 on the linearity of the product with a matrix,

\[\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P) = \mat V\,(h\,\vek n) + \vek R = h\,(\mat V\vek n) + \vek R ,\]

where \(\vek R\) is the column of the remainders \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(R_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(R_{\mathrm{z}}\). We divide both sides by \(h\):

\[\frac{1}{h}\,\big(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\big) = \mat V\vek n + \frac{1}{h}\,\vek R .\]

The remainders divided by the length of the fibre go to zero as the fibre gets shorter (theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step), so the left side approaches the column \(\mat V\vek n\). Let us compute it. We write the matrix, the vector and the result together, and compute the rows below by (1.38):

\[\mat V\vek n = \begin{bmatrix} 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} & -4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} & 0 \\ 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac13 \\ \tfrac23 \\ \tfrac23 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6{,}5035 \cdot 10^{-7} \\ -3{,}9024 \cdot 10^{-7} \\ -3{,}9040 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} .\]

Each entry of the result is the corresponding row of the matrix times the same column:

  1. Row \(x\): \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot \tfrac13 + (-4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}) \cdot \tfrac23 + 0 \cdot \tfrac23 = 6{,}5067 \cdot 10^{-7} - 3{,}123 \cdot 10^{-10} = 6{,}5035 \cdot 10^{-7}\).
  2. Row \(y\): \(4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} \cdot \tfrac13 + (-5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}) \cdot \tfrac23 + 0 \cdot \tfrac23 = 1{,}562 \cdot 10^{-10} - 3{,}9040 \cdot 10^{-7} = -3{,}9024 \cdot 10^{-7}\).
  3. Row \(z\): \(0 \cdot \tfrac13 + 0 \cdot \tfrac23 + (-5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}) \cdot \tfrac23 = -3{,}9040 \cdot 10^{-7}\).

Let us draw the fibre. The triple of axes at the top right shows that the axis \(x\) points down, the axis \(y\) to the right and the axis \(z\) obliquely towards the reader. The grey dashed vertical line on the left is the axis of the bar. The point \(P\) is the start of the fibre, to the right of the axis, because it is 4 mm from it. The thick line from \(P\) is the fibre with the vector \(h\,\vek n\). The point \(Q\) is its other end. It lies lower and farther from the axis than \(P\), because all three components of \(\vek n\) are positive. The blue dimension line with limit ticks is the difference of displacements of the ends, \(h\,\mat V\vek n\). It is drawn from \(Q\) onward so that it does not overlap the fibre, because the difference is a vector that has a direction and a length, and we choose its start. It is strongly enlarged, because in reality it would be more than a thousand times shorter than the fibre. The grey dashed segments build it from three parts along the axes. The first part points down in the direction of the axis \(x\), because the component \(x\) is positive. It is followed by the part against the direction of the axis \(y\) and the part against the direction of the axis \(z\), because these components are negative. Both point towards the axis of the bar.

The first number is the value \(6{,}5035 \cdot 10^{-7}\) that we approached with ever shorter fibres in section 1.7.3. There we computed it only for the component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), while the product gives all three at once. What do they say? A fibre of length 1 mm, \(h = 0{,}001\) m, has the difference of displacements of the ends of the fibre of about \(h\,\mat V\vek n\), that is, \(6{,}5035 \cdot 10^{-10}\) m in the direction of the axis \(x\) and \(-3{,}9024 \cdot 10^{-10}\) m and \(-3{,}9040 \cdot 10^{-10}\) m in the directions of the axes \(y\) and \(z\) (figure 1.322, parts along the axes). The end \(Q\) lies lower than \(P\), where the bar moves down more under its own weight, so the component \(x\) is positive and the fibre lengthens in the direction of the axis of the bar. The end \(Q\) also lies farther from the axis of the bar than \(P\), and the bar gets thinner, so \(Q\) moves toward the axis more than \(P\) does: the components \(y\) and \(z\) are negative.

Why are the components \(y\) and \(z\) nearly equal, but not quite? The main part of both is \(-5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot \tfrac23 = -3{,}9040 \cdot 10^{-7}\). The bar thins by the same amount in both transverse directions, which the two equal entries \(-5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\) on the main diagonal in rows \(y\) and \(z\) express, and the vector \(\vek n\) has the same component \(\tfrac23\) in both directions. The component \(y\) gets the extra term \(1{,}562 \cdot 10^{-10}\) from the entry in row \(y\) and column \(x\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y_{\mathrm{P}}\), where \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\) m⁻¹ and the number \(0{,}6\) is the thinning ratio \(0{,}3\) of steel times the \(2\) of the strain \(2a\,(L - x)\) along the bar (section 1.7.1). The end \(Q\) lies \(h/3\) deeper than \(P\), where the difference \(L - x\) is smaller, so the bar thins a little less, and so a point at the distance \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\) from the axis moves toward the axis a little less there. The component \(z\) has no such term. The point \(P\) lies in the plane \(z = 0\), where \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z\) is zero at every depth, so there \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\).

For the cube the equalities of lemma 1.97 are exact, because there are no remainders. For the hanging bar, however, the lemma holds only for the part of the difference of displacements that the matrix \(\mat V\) gives, and the remainders do not follow it. For the fibre from the point \(P\) in the direction \(\vek n\) we computed for the component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) in section 1.7.3: at a length of 1 mm the part with the partial derivatives is \(6{,}504 \cdot 10^{-10}\) m (more precisely \(6{,}5035 \cdot 10^{-10}\) m) and the remainder \(R_{\mathrm{x}} = -7{,}374 \cdot 10^{-14}\) m, at a length of 0.1 mm they are \(6{,}504 \cdot 10^{-11}\) m and \(-7{,}374 \cdot 10^{-16}\) m. For a fibre ten times shorter the part with the matrix is ten times smaller, as the second equality of the lemma requires, while the remainder is a hundred times smaller, because each of its terms is a product of two components of the step. So the lemma describes exactly the part of the difference of displacements that dominates for short fibres.

1.16.3 The product of matrices

Let us return to the sheared cube, glued to the table, whose top face we pushed sideways by a thousandth of its height. Its matrix \(\mat K\) has a single nonzero entry, \(0{,}001\) in row \(x\) and column \(z\), and for every fibre with the vector \(\vek v\) it gives the difference of displacements of its ends \(\mat K\vek v\) with the components \(0{,}001\,v_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(0\) and \(0\). The vector of the fibre after loading is its vector before loading plus this difference: \(\vek v + \mat K\vek v\) has the components \(v_{\mathrm{x}} + 0{,}001\,v_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\). This vector, too, is the product with a single matrix. The entry \(x\) of the result is \(1 \cdot v_{\mathrm{x}} + 0 \cdot v_{\mathrm{y}} + 0{,}001 \cdot v_{\mathrm{z}}\), which is the row with the entries \(1\), \(0\) and \(0{,}001\) times the column \(\vek v\), and we get the other two rows in the same way:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0{,}001 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} v_{\mathrm{x}} \\ v_{\mathrm{y}} \\ v_{\mathrm{z}} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} v_{\mathrm{x}} + 0{,}001\,v_{\mathrm{z}} \\ v_{\mathrm{y}} \\ v_{\mathrm{z}} \end{bmatrix} .\]

Such a matrix tells where the vector of every fibre goes. But what if we deform a piece of material twice in a row, first in one way and then in another? The vector of a fibre after the first deformation is the input of the second. Is the combined rule again the product with a single matrix, and with which one?

Let us take a simple example with large numbers, so that the picture is clear (figure 1.323). Let the first rule double the component \(x\) of every vector and leave the other two. This is a stretching in the direction of the axis \(x\) to twice the length. Let the second rule add the component \(z\) to the component \(x\) and leave the other two. This is a shear like the shear of the cube, only with the ratio \(1\) instead of \(0{,}001\). By (1.38) we write them with the matrices

\[\mat D = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat G = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

since \(\mat D\vek v = (2\,v_{\mathrm{x}},\ v_{\mathrm{y}},\ v_{\mathrm{z}})\) and \(\mat G\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{z}},\ v_{\mathrm{y}},\ v_{\mathrm{z}})\). Figure 1.323 shows a square in the plane \(x\)-\(z\) that we first shear and then stretch, and a square that we first stretch and then shear.

Let us draw the top row. The axes on the left show that the axis \(x\) points to the right and the axis \(z\) up. The blackwhite square with a grid is a square in the plane \(x\)-\(z\) before any deformation. The grid divides it into four parts, so that it can be seen how the square changes. The blue arrow along its left edge is the vector of this edge, \((0, 0, 1)\). We follow it through all the steps. The arrow \(\mat G\) means that we first shear the square. The grey parallelogram is the square after the shear. The bottom edge stays, the top one moves by \(1\) to the right, because \(\mat G\) adds the component \(z\) to the component \(x\), and that is \(0\) at the bottom and \(1\) at the top. The blue arrow is therefore now tilted, \((1, 0, 1)\). The arrow \(\mat D\) means that we then stretch the square. The orange parallelogram is the result of both steps. Each component \(x\) is doubled, so the shape is twice as wide. The final blue arrow is \(\mat D(1, 0, 1) = (2, 0, 1)\), which is written above it.

The bottom row starts with the same blackwhite square and the same blue arrow, only now \(\mat D\) acts first. The arrow \(\mat D\) means stretching. The grey rectangle is twice as wide as the square. The blue arrow stays vertical, since \(\mat D\) does not change the vector \((0, 0, 1)\), because its component \(x\) is zero. The arrow \(\mat G\) means the shear. The orange parallelogram is the result. The top edge moves only by \(1\) to the right and reaches from \(1\) to \(3\), while in the top row it reached from \(2\) to \(4\). The final blue arrow is \(\mat G(0, 0, 1) = (1, 0, 1)\). The two orange shapes are different, so the order matters.

How one entry of the product is computed is shown in figure 1.324 on the matrices \(\mat D\) and \(\mat G\), which we will compute below.

Let us draw the top row. On the left is the matrix \(\mat D\), after it the sign \(\times\) and the matrix \(\mat G\). The sign \(=\) leads to the product \(\mat D\mat G\), whose entries we are only now computing. We compute the entry in row \(x\) and column \(z\). So marked in blue are row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat D\), with the letter \(x\) on the left, and column \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat G\), with the letter \(z\) above it. The same place in the product is the blue entry. Under the matrices is the computation: we multiply the entries at the same positions of the row and the column and add the products, \(2 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 1 = 2\). The result is the blue entry of the product.

The bottom row computes the same entry for the reverse order. Now the left factor is the matrix \(\mat G\) with the sign \(\times\), the right factor is the matrix \(\mat D\) and the product \(\mat G\mat D\) is after the sign \(=\). Marked in blue are row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat G\) and column \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat D\), and the blue entry is again at the place \((x, z)\) of the product. The computation is \(1 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1 = 1\). The same entry is \(2\) at the top and \(1\) at the bottom, so the products differ.

Let us find the matrix for two rules one after the other in general (figure 1.325). Let \(\mat A\) and \(\mat B\) be square matrices of order \(3\). We first multiply the vector \(\vek v\) by \(\mat B\) and get \(\vek y = \mat B\vek v\), then we multiply \(\vek y\) by \(\mat A\) and get \(\vek w = \mat A\vek y = \mat A\,(\mat B\vek v)\). Let us express the entry \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) through the components of the vector \(\vek v\). The figure does this step by step. The upper part is the entry \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) as a sum of three lines: each is the entry \(A_{\mathrm{xj}}\) of the matrix \(\mat A\) times the entry \(y_{\mathrm{j}}\) of the column \(\vek y\), which is expanded in the entries of the matrix \(\mat B\) and the components of \(\vek v\). The lower table is the same expression with the brackets expanded: nine terms, in each row the terms of the same line above. Above the columns are the components \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) that the terms contain. Each column is coloured separately, because we will collect the terms by columns. The three small matrices on the right show which row of the matrix \(\mat A\) we take for \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), for \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and for \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\).

  1. By (1.38), \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = A_{\mathrm{xx}}\,y_{\mathrm{x}} + A_{\mathrm{xy}}\,y_{\mathrm{y}} + A_{\mathrm{xz}}\,y_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  2. By the same equation the entries of the column \(\vek y = \mat B\vek v\) are \(y_{\mathrm{x}} = B_{\mathrm{xx}}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} + B_{\mathrm{xy}}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} + B_{\mathrm{xz}}\,v_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(y_{\mathrm{y}} = B_{\mathrm{yx}}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} + B_{\mathrm{yy}}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} + B_{\mathrm{yz}}\,v_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{z}} = B_{\mathrm{zx}}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} + B_{\mathrm{zy}}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} + B_{\mathrm{zz}}\,v_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  3. We put these three expressions into step 1 and expand each product by the rule for multiplying a sum by a number. We get nine terms, each the product of one entry of the matrix \(\mat A\), one entry of the matrix \(\mat B\) and one component of the vector \(\vek v\):
    \[\begin{aligned} w_{\mathrm{x}} &= A_{\mathrm{xx}}B_{\mathrm{xx}}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} + A_{\mathrm{xx}}B_{\mathrm{xy}}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} + A_{\mathrm{xx}}B_{\mathrm{xz}}\,v_{\mathrm{z}} \\ &\quad + A_{\mathrm{xy}}B_{\mathrm{yx}}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} + A_{\mathrm{xy}}B_{\mathrm{yy}}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} + A_{\mathrm{xy}}B_{\mathrm{yz}}\,v_{\mathrm{z}} \\ &\quad + A_{\mathrm{xz}}B_{\mathrm{zx}}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} + A_{\mathrm{xz}}B_{\mathrm{zy}}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} + A_{\mathrm{xz}}B_{\mathrm{zz}}\,v_{\mathrm{z}} . \end{aligned}\]
  4. We collect the three terms with \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is the first column of the expression in step 3, and take \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) out: \((A_{\mathrm{xx}}\,B_{\mathrm{xx}} + A_{\mathrm{xy}}\,B_{\mathrm{yx}} + A_{\mathrm{xz}}\,B_{\mathrm{zx}})\,v_{\mathrm{x}}\). In the same way we collect the terms with \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\), which give \((A_{\mathrm{xx}}\,B_{\mathrm{xy}} + A_{\mathrm{xy}}\,B_{\mathrm{yy}} + A_{\mathrm{xz}}\,B_{\mathrm{zy}})\,v_{\mathrm{y}}\), and the terms with \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\), which give \((A_{\mathrm{xx}}\,B_{\mathrm{xz}} + A_{\mathrm{xy}}\,B_{\mathrm{yz}} + A_{\mathrm{xz}}\,B_{\mathrm{zz}})\,v_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  5. The number in front of \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) is row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat A\) times column \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat B\) (as in figure 1.324), since we walk along the row \(A_{\mathrm{xx}}, A_{\mathrm{xy}}, A_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and down the column \(B_{\mathrm{xx}}, B_{\mathrm{yx}}, B_{\mathrm{zx}}\). The number in front of \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) is the same row times column \(y\) of the matrix \(\mat B\), and the number in front of \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) the same row times column \(z\).
  6. For \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) the calculation is the same, only with row \(y\) or \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat A\) in place of row \(x\).

So the vector \(\mat A\,(\mat B\vek v)\) is the product of a single matrix with the vector \(\vek v\). The entry of this matrix in row \(i\) and column \(k\) is row \(i\) of the matrix \(\mat A\) times column \(k\) of the matrix \(\mat B\), that is, \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}}\). This matrix is the product of the two matrices.

Definition 1.98 Matrix product (produkt matrik)

Let \(\mat A\) be a matrix of size \(m \times n\) and \(\mat B\) a matrix of size \(n \times p\). Their product (produkt) \(\mat A\mat B\) is the matrix of size \(m \times p\) with the entries

\[\begin{aligned} (\mat A\mat B)_{\mathrm{ik}} &= \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}} = A_{\mathrm{i}1}\,B_{1\mathrm{k}} + A_{\mathrm{i}2}\,B_{2\mathrm{k}} + \dots + A_{\mathrm{in}}\,B_{\mathrm{nk}} , \\ &\qquad i = 1, \dots, m , \quad k = 1, \dots, p . \end{aligned} \tag{1.40}\]

So the entry at the position \((i, k)\) is row \(i\) of the matrix \(\mat A\) times column \(k\) of the matrix \(\mat B\). For \(p = 1\) the matrix \(\mat B\) is a column, and \(\mat A\mat B\) is the product of a matrix and a vector of definition 1.96.

Source: KREYSZIG §7.2, (1) (PDF p. 289), the idea with two rules one after the other on PDF pp. 291-292, CM (2.3.6) (PDF p. 63).

The product \(\mat A\mat B\) exists only if \(\mat A\) has as many columns as \(\mat B\) has rows, since every entry of a row of the matrix \(\mat A\) must get its partner in a column of the matrix \(\mat B\). We read \(\mat A\mat B\) from right to left: first \(\mat B\) acts, then \(\mat A\), as in \(\mat A\,(\mat B\vek v)\). Let us compute both products of the matrices \(\mat D\) and \(\mat G\). The entry in row \(x\) and column \(z\) of the product \(\mat D\mat G\) is row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat D\), \((2, 0, 0)\), times column \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat G\), \((1, 0, 1)\), that is, \(2 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 1 = 2\). The same entry of the product \(\mat G\mat D\) is row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat G\), \((1, 0, 1)\), times column \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat D\), \((0, 0, 1)\), that is, \(1 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1 = 1\). When we compute all nine entries, we get

\[\mat D\mat G = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat G\mat D = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The matrices differ in the entry we computed. In figure 1.323 we see this on the left vertical edge with the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 0, 1)\). With \(\mat D\mat G\) the shear first tilts it to \((1, 0, 1)\), and then the stretching doubles its horizontal part too, so the edge ends as \((2, 0, 1)\). With \(\mat G\mat D\) the stretching does not change the vertical edge, because it has no horizontal part, and the shear then tilts it to \((1, 0, 1)\). Stretching followed by shear is not the same as shear followed by stretching.

Which laws of arithmetic for numbers hold for the matrix product as well, and which do not, the next lemma tells.

Let us first look at them on one vector (figure 1.326).

Let us draw the upper half. The axes \(x\) and \(z\) define the plane. The path shows the tip of the vector \(\vek v = (1, 0, 1)\), which we map three times. The step \(\mat C\) is a shear that adds the component \(z\) to the component \(x\), and the tip goes to \((2, 0, 1)\). The step \(\mat B\) doubles the component \(x\), to \((4, 0, 1)\). The step \(\mat A\) doubles the component \(z\), to \((4, 0, 2)\). The blue arrow skips the intermediate point after two steps: the tip goes from \(\mat C\vek v\) to \(\mat A\mat B\mat C\vek v\) with the single matrix \(\mat A\mat B\). The orange arrow skips the first two steps with the matrix \(\mat B\mat C\). The lower half uses three other matrices: \(\mat B\) doubles the component \(x\), \(\mat C\) doubles the component \(z\), and \(\mat A\) is a shear. On the left are the image \(\mat B\vek v = (2, 0, 1)\) (blue) and the image \(\mat C\vek v = (1, 0, 2)\) (orange), their sum is the blackwhite arrow \((\mat B + \mat C)\vek v = (3, 0, 3)\), and the grey dashed lines complete the parallelogram. The arrow \(\mat A\) leads to the right picture, where the shear moves all three arrows: \(\mat A\mat B\vek v = (3, 0, 1)\), \(\mat A\mat C\vek v = (3, 0, 2)\) and their sum \(\mat A\,(\mat B + \mat C)\vek v = (6, 0, 3)\).

Lemma 1.99 Properties of the matrix product (lastnosti produkta matrik)

For matrices whose sizes allow the sums and products below, and for every number \(c\):

  1. \((\mat A\mat B)\,\vek v = \mat A\,(\mat B\vek v)\) for every column \(\vek v\),
  2. \((\mat A\mat B)\,\mat C = \mat A\,(\mat B\mat C)\),
  3. \(\mat A\,(\mat B + \mat C) = \mat A\mat B + \mat A\mat C\), \((\mat A + \mat B)\,\mat C = \mat A\mat C + \mat B\mat C\) and \((c\,\mat A)\,\mat B = c\,(\mat A\mat B) = \mat A\,(c\,\mat B)\),
  4. there are square matrices \(\mat A\) and \(\mat B\) of the same order with \(\mat A\mat B \neq \mat B\mat A\).
Proof

We must show four items. The first three are equalities of matrices, so we check them entry by entry (definition 1.93), the fourth with an example.

1. Products one after the other.

  1. Let \(\mat A\) be of size \(m \times n\), \(\mat B\) of size \(n \times p\) and \(\vek v\) a column with \(p\) entries. Both sides are columns with \(m\) entries. We compare the entry \(i\).
  2. By (1.38) the entry \(j\) of the column \(\mat B\vek v\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{p} B_{\mathrm{jk}}\,v_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  3. By the same equation the entry \(i\) of the column \(\mat A\,(\mat B\vek v)\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{p} B_{\mathrm{jk}}\,v_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  4. We multiply the factor \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\) into the inner sum by the rule for multiplying a sum by a number. We get a sum of \(n \cdot p\) terms \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}}\,v_{\mathrm{k}}\), one for each pair of indices \(j\) and \(k\).
  5. A sum of finitely many numbers does not depend on the order of adding, so we add the terms in another order, first over \(j\) and then over \(k\): \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{p} \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}}\,v_{\mathrm{k}}\). For \(n = p = 2\) the terms are in a table with the rows \(j = 1, 2\) and the columns \(k = 1, 2\):
    \[\begin{array}{cc} A_{\mathrm{i}1}B_{11}v_1 & A_{\mathrm{i}1}B_{12}v_2 \\ A_{\mathrm{i}2}B_{21}v_1 & A_{\mathrm{i}2}B_{22}v_2 \end{array}\]
    Before, we added by rows, now first by columns, and the sum of all four terms is the same.
  6. In the inner sum \(v_{\mathrm{k}}\) is a common factor of all terms, so we take it out: \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{p} \big(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}}\big)\,v_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  7. By (1.40) the bracket is the entry \((\mat A\mat B)_{\mathrm{ik}}\), so by (1.38) the sum is the entry \(i\) of the column \((\mat A\mat B)\,\vek v\).

2. Grouping.

  1. Let \(\mat A\) be of size \(m \times n\), \(\mat B\) of size \(n \times p\) and \(\mat C\) of size \(p \times q\). Both sides are matrices of size \(m \times q\) (definition 1.98). We compare the entry \((i, l)\).
  2. By (1.40), used twice, the entry \((i, l)\) of the left side is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{p} \big(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}}\big)\,C_{\mathrm{kl}}\).
  3. We multiply the factor \(C_{\mathrm{kl}}\) into the bracket. We get the sum of the terms \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}}\,C_{\mathrm{kl}}\) over all pairs \(j\) and \(k\).
  4. We change the order of adding as in item 1, step 5: \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{p} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}}\,C_{\mathrm{kl}}\).
  5. In the inner sum \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is a common factor, so we take it out: \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}} \big(\sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{p} B_{\mathrm{jk}}\,C_{\mathrm{kl}}\big)\).
  6. The bracket is the entry \((\mat B\mat C)_{\mathrm{jl}}\), so the sum is the entry \((i, l)\) of the matrix \(\mat A\,(\mat B\mat C)\) ((1.40)).

3. Distributing and multiples.

  1. By (1.40) and definition 1.94 the entry \((i, k)\) of the matrix \(\mat A\,(\mat B + \mat C)\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,(B_{\mathrm{jk}} + C_{\mathrm{jk}})\).
  2. We expand each term, \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,(B_{\mathrm{jk}} + C_{\mathrm{jk}}) = A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}} + A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,C_{\mathrm{jk}}\), and arrange the terms in two sums, \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,C_{\mathrm{jk}}\). This is \((\mat A\mat B)_{\mathrm{ik}} + (\mat A\mat C)_{\mathrm{ik}}\), the entry of the matrix \(\mat A\mat B + \mat A\mat C\).
  3. In the same way the entry \((i, k)\) of the matrix \((\mat A + \mat B)\,\mat C\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} (A_{\mathrm{ij}} + B_{\mathrm{ij}})\,C_{\mathrm{jk}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,C_{\mathrm{jk}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} B_{\mathrm{ij}}\,C_{\mathrm{jk}}\), the entry of the matrix \(\mat A\mat C + \mat B\mat C\). We need both equalities separately, because we may not change the order of the factors in a matrix product, as item 4 shows.
  4. The entry \((i, k)\) of the matrix \((c\,\mat A)\,\mat B\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} c\,A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}}\), that of the matrix \(\mat A\,(c\,\mat B)\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,c\,B_{\mathrm{jk}}\). In both sums \(c\) is a common factor of all terms. Taking it out, we get \(c \sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}}\), the entry of the matrix \(c\,(\mat A\mat B)\).

4. The order of the factors.

  1. Take the square matrices of order \(3\)
    \[\mat D = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat G = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]
  2. By (1.40) the entry in row \(x\) and column \(z\) of the product \(\mat D\mat G\) is the row \((2, 0, 0)\) times the column \((1, 0, 1)\), that is, \(2 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 1 = 2\).
  3. The entry at the same position of the product \(\mat G\mat D\) is the row \((1, 0, 1)\) times the column \((0, 0, 1)\), that is, \(1 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1 = 1\).
  4. The matrices \(\mat D\mat G\) and \(\mat G\mat D\) do not agree in all entries at the same positions, so they are not equal (definition 1.93). The matrices \(\mat A = \mat D\) and \(\mat B = \mat G\) are the pair we wanted.

Source: KREYSZIG §7.2, (2a) to (2d) and Example 4 (PDF p. 290), CM §2.3.5, remarks (4) and (7) (PDF p. 64).

The proof of items 1, 2 and 3 rests on adding the same terms in a different order and on expanding terms. Figure 1.327 shows the first.

Let us draw the upper half. The rectangles show the shapes of the factors: \(\mat A\) is \(m \times n\), \(\mat B\) is \(n \times p\) and \(\vek v\) is \(p \times 1\), the result is a column with \(m\) entries. The table has the terms \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}}\,v_{\mathrm{k}}\), with row \(j\) and column \(k\), four of them for \(n = p = 2\). The orange rows add the terms row by row: the row \(j\) is \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\) times the entry \(j\) of the column \(\mat B\vek v\), and the sum of the rows is the entry \(i\) of the vector \(\mat A\,(\mat B\vek v)\). The blue columns add the same terms column by column: in the column \(k\) the common factor is \(v_{\mathrm{k}}\), in front of it stands the entry \((\mat A\mat B)_{\mathrm{ik}}\), and the sum of the columns is the entry \(i\) of the vector \((\mat A\mat B)\vek v\). The lower half has the same form. The rectangles show that \(\mat A\mat B\mat C\) is of size \(m \times q\). The table has the terms \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}}\,C_{\mathrm{kl}}\), the orange rows give the entry \((i, l)\) of the matrix \(\mat A\,(\mat B\mat C)\) and the blue columns the same entry of the matrix \((\mat A\mat B)\,\mat C\).

The expanding of terms in item 3 is shown by figure 1.328.

Let us draw the upper table. On the left is the term \(j\) of the sum for the entry \((i, k)\) of the matrix \(\mat A\,(\mat B + \mat C)\), that is \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,(B_{\mathrm{jk}} + C_{\mathrm{jk}})\). On the right each term is expanded into two. The sums below the line are the entries \((i, k)\) of the matrices \(\mat A\mat B\) and \(\mat A\mat C\). The middle is the same for \((\mat A + \mat B)\,\mat C\), with the expansion and the sum as above. Below are the terms for \((c\,\mat A)\,\mat B\) and for \(\mat A\,(c\,\mat B)\): the numbers in each row are equal, because when multiplying all three numbers the order does not matter. The sums below the line agree, and \(c\) stands in front of the sum.

Item 1 is the reason for the definition: the matrix product is a single matrix that does the same as both matrices one after the other. Item 2 says that with three rules one after the other it does not matter which two we combine into one matrix first, so we write no brackets and write \(\mat A\mat B\mat C\). Item 4, however, warns of a difference from numbers. For numbers \(2 \cdot 3 = 3 \cdot 2\), but for matrices we may not in general change the order of the factors, because two deformations one after the other in the reverse order are a different deformation, as we saw in figure 1.323. For some pairs of matrices the product is the same in both orders, for example for two matrices whose nonzero entries all lie on the main diagonal, like \(\mat D\). Such matrices, call them \(\mat A\) and \(\mat B\), stretch a vector along the axes, and it does not matter which stretching we do first. By calculation: in the sum \((\mat A\mat B)_{\mathrm{ik}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{jk}}\) at most the term with \(j = i = k\) is nonzero, so the product has nonzero entries only on the main diagonal, namely \(A_{\mathrm{ii}}\,B_{\mathrm{ii}}\). For the product \(\mat B\mat A\) these are \(B_{\mathrm{ii}}\,A_{\mathrm{ii}}\), the same numbers.

1.16.4 The transposed matrix and the split

In section 1.7.2 we noticed in the table of partial derivatives of the hanging bar pairs off the main diagonal that are equal in size and opposite in sign: \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,y\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y\). In the matrix \(\mat V\) of section 1.16.2 this is the pair in row \(x\) and column \(y\) and in row \(y\) and column \(x\):

\[\mat V = \begin{bmatrix} 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} & -4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} & 0 \\ 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} .\]

We showed that such a pair means a small turn of the material without shear. The two entries of such a pair lie in the matrix as mirror images across the main diagonal: the first in row \(x\) and column \(y\), the second in row \(y\) and column \(x\). To compare a matrix with its mirror image, we need a matrix in which the rows and the columns exchange their roles. The split that follows will separate the part of the matrix that stretches the material from the part that turns it.

Definition 1.100 Transposed matrix (transponirana matrika)

For a matrix \(\mat A\) of size \(m \times n\) the transposed matrix \(\mat A^\T\) (transponirana matrika) is the matrix of size \(n \times m\) with the entries

\[(\mat A^\T)_{\mathrm{ij}} = A_{\mathrm{ji}} , \qquad i = 1, \dots, n , \quad j = 1, \dots, m .\]

So row \(i\) of the matrix \(\mat A^\T\) is column \(i\) of the matrix \(\mat A\). A column \(\vek v\) with \(n\) entries thereby becomes the row \(\vek v^\T = [\,v_1\ \ v_2\ \cdots\ v_{\mathrm{n}}\,]\).

Source: KREYSZIG §7.2, (9) (PDF pp. 292-293), CM §2.3.3 (PDF p. 62).

For a square matrix, transposition replaces every entry by its mirror image across the main diagonal, while the entries on the main diagonal stay in place, because for them \(i = j\) (figure 1.329). For the sheared cube, the only nonzero entry of its matrix \(\mat K\) moves from row \(x\) and column \(z\) to row \(z\) and column \(x\):

\[\mat K^\T = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0{,}001 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

For the hanging bar, the two entries of the pair in the matrix \(\mat V\) of its partial derivatives at the point \(P\) (section 1.16.2) swap places: in \(\mat V^\T\) the entry \(-4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}\) is in row \(y\) and column \(x\), and \(4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}\) in row \(x\) and column \(y\). We read \(\mat A^\T\) as "A transposed".

Let us draw this with the numbers \(1\) to \(9\). On the left is the matrix \(\mat A\), in which the numbers fill the rows in order. The blue shaded first row is \(1, 2, 3\). The arrow leads to the transposed matrix \(\mat A^\T\) on the right, in which the same triple is the blue shaded first column: the row has become a column. The grey dashed lines in both matrices join the numbers \(1\), \(5\) and \(9\), that is the main diagonal. These numbers stay in place, because for them the row equals the column. Every other number moves to the mirror position across the diagonal. As an example, in both matrices the number \(6\) is circled. In \(\mat A\) it is in row \(2\) and column \(3\), in \(\mat A^\T\) in row \(3\) and column \(2\).

Transposing twice gives back the original matrix, since every entry is mirrored twice. With sums and products it gets along as follows.

Lemma 1.101 Transposing a sum, a multiple and a product (transponiranje vsote, večkratnika in produkta)

For matrices whose sizes allow the sums and products below, and for every number \(c\):

  1. \((\mat A^\T)^\T = \mat A\),
  2. \((\mat A + \mat B)^\T = \mat A^\T + \mat B^\T\) and \((c\,\mat A)^\T = c\,\mat A^\T\),
  3. \((\mat A\mat B)^\T = \mat B^\T\mat A^\T\),
  4. for a column \(\vek v\) with \(m\) entries, a matrix \(\mat A\) of size \(m \times n\) and a column \(\vek w\) with \(n\) entries, \(\vek v^\T\mat A\vek w\) is a matrix of size \(1 \times 1\) whose only entry is
    \[\vek v^\T\mat A\vek w = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{m} \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} v_{\mathrm{i}}\,A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,w_{\mathrm{j}} . \tag{1.41}\]
Proof

We must show four items. The first three are equalities of matrices, which we check entry by entry (definition 1.93), and in the fourth we compute the only entry.

1. Transposing twice.

  1. Let \(\mat A\) be of size \(m \times n\). Then \(\mat A^\T\) is of size \(n \times m\) and \((\mat A^\T)^\T\) of size \(m \times n\), the same as \(\mat A\).
  2. By definition 1.100, used twice, \(\big((\mat A^\T)^\T\big)_{\mathrm{ij}} = (\mat A^\T)_{\mathrm{ji}} = A_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

2. Sum and multiple.

  1. By definition 1.100 and definition 1.94, \(\big((\mat A + \mat B)^\T\big)_{\mathrm{ij}} = (\mat A + \mat B)_{\mathrm{ji}} = A_{\mathrm{ji}} + B_{\mathrm{ji}}\).
  2. By definition 1.100, \(A_{\mathrm{ji}} + B_{\mathrm{ji}} = (\mat A^\T)_{\mathrm{ij}} + (\mat B^\T)_{\mathrm{ij}}\), which is the entry \((i, j)\) of the matrix \(\mat A^\T + \mat B^\T\).
  3. In the same way, \(\big((c\,\mat A)^\T\big)_{\mathrm{ij}} = (c\,\mat A)_{\mathrm{ji}} = c\,A_{\mathrm{ji}} = c\,(\mat A^\T)_{\mathrm{ij}}\), the entry of the matrix \(c\,\mat A^\T\).

3. Product.

  1. Let \(\mat A\) be of size \(m \times n\) and \(\mat B\) of size \(n \times p\). The matrix \(\mat A\mat B\) is of size \(m \times p\), so \((\mat A\mat B)^\T\) is of size \(p \times m\). The matrix \(\mat B^\T\) is of size \(p \times n\) and \(\mat A^\T\) of size \(n \times m\), so the product \(\mat B^\T\mat A^\T\) exists and is of size \(p \times m\).
  2. By definition 1.100, \(\big((\mat A\mat B)^\T\big)_{\mathrm{ik}} = (\mat A\mat B)_{\mathrm{ki}}\).
  3. By (1.40), \((\mat A\mat B)_{\mathrm{ki}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{kj}}\,B_{\mathrm{ji}}\).
  4. In each term we change the order of the factors, which we may do for numbers: \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} B_{\mathrm{ji}}\,A_{\mathrm{kj}}\).
  5. By definition 1.100, \(B_{\mathrm{ji}} = (\mat B^\T)_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{kj}} = (\mat A^\T)_{\mathrm{jk}}\), so the sum equals \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} (\mat B^\T)_{\mathrm{ij}}\,(\mat A^\T)_{\mathrm{jk}}\).
  6. By (1.40) this is the entry \((i, k)\) of the matrix \(\mat B^\T\mat A^\T\).

4. The double sum.

  1. The column \(\mat A\vek w\) has \(m\) entries, and by (1.38) its entry \(i\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,w_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  2. The row \(\vek v^\T\) is a matrix of size \(1 \times m\), so the product \(\vek v^\T\,(\mat A\vek w)\) is by definition 1.98 a matrix of size \(1 \times 1\). By item 2 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product it equals the matrix \((\vek v^\T\mat A)\,\vek w\), so we write no brackets.
  3. By (1.40) its only entry is the row \(\vek v^\T\) times the column \(\mat A\vek w\): \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{m} v_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,w_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  4. We multiply the factor \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) into the inner sum by the rule for multiplying a sum by a number and get (1.41).

Source: KREYSZIG §7.2, (10a) to (10d) (PDF p. 293), CM §2.3.3 and §2.3.5, remark (9) (PDF pp. 62 and 64), KREYSZIG §8.4, (7) (PDF p. 369) for item 4.

We test these rules on numbers (figure 1.330).

Let us draw the upper part. The first row of rectangles: \(\mat A\) is \(m \times n\), after transposing \(n \times m\) and after the second time \(m \times n\) again. The second row shows the product \(\mat A\mat B\) of size \(m \times p\) and its transposed matrix of size \(p \times m\), the third the product \(\mat B^\T\mat A^\T\), which is also \(p \times m\). Below we compute on the numbers \(\mat A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mat B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). The first row of numbers is \((\mat A + \mat B)^\T\) and \(\mat A^\T + \mat B^\T\): the blue entry at the position \((1, 2)\) is in both equal to \(A_{21} + B_{21} = 1\). The next row shows the same for the double. The first row of the product computes the entry \((2, 1)\) of the matrix \(\mat A\mat B\): shaded in blue are the row \(2\) of the matrix \(\mat A\) and the column \(1\) of the matrix \(\mat B\), the result is \(-3\), which moves to the position \((1, 2)\) under transposition. The last row gets the same entry as the row \(1\) of the matrix \(\mat B^\T\), which is the column \(1\) of the matrix \(\mat B\), times the column \(2\) of the matrix \(\mat A^\T\), which is the row \(2\) of the matrix \(\mat A\).

Item 4 is shown by figure 1.331.

Let us draw the upper row. The row \(\vek v^\T\) has the entries \(v_1\), \(v_2\), \(v_3\), the matrix \(\mat A\) nine entries and the column \(\vek w\) the entries \(w_1\), \(w_2\), \(w_3\). We choose the entry \(A_{23}\), circled in blue. It is multiplied by the blue \(v_2\), because it lies in the row \(2\), and by the orange \(w_3\), because it lies in the column \(3\). The middle row computes in two steps: the column \(\mat A\vek w\) has \(m\) entries, and the row \(\vek v^\T\) multiplies them by the matching ones, the result is a \(1 \times 1\) matrix. The table below lists the nine terms \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\,A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,w_{\mathrm{j}}\). Each row has the common factor \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) and is \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\mat A\vek w)_{\mathrm{i}}\), the orange column holds the terms with \(w_3\), the sum of all terms is \(\vek v^\T\mat A\vek w\).

In item 3 the order is reversed. Why? Transposition exchanges rows and columns, and an entry of a product is a row of the first matrix times a column of the second. After the exchange the rows of the first matrix become columns, and for the product to be row times column again, the transposed first matrix must stand on the right.

We will identify the matrix of size \(1 \times 1\) of item 4 with its only entry, since a table with a single number holds exactly that number and we calculate with it as with the number. The double sum (1.41) has \(m \cdot n\) terms, one for each entry of the matrix. Each entry \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is multiplied by the entry \(i\) of the column on the left and the entry \(j\) of the column on the right. Without a matrix in between, the product of a row and a column with three entries is by (1.40) \(\vek v^\T\vek w = v_{\mathrm{x}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,w_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}\,w_{\mathrm{z}}\), and for \(\vek w = \vek v\) it is \(\vek v^\T\vek v = v_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + v_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + v_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = |\vek v|^2\) by (1.10). The sum of the products of matching components of two vectors will appear in chapter 2 as a concept of its own with a geometric meaning.

Now we can name the matrices that do not change under transposition or only change their sign. Figure 1.332 shows examples.

Definition 1.102 Symmetric and antisymmetric matrix (simetrična in antisimetrična matrika)

A square matrix \(\mat A\) is symmetric (simetrična) if \(\mat A^\T = \mat A\), that is, \(A_{\mathrm{ij}} = A_{\mathrm{ji}}\) for all \(i\) and \(j\), and antisymmetric (antisimetrična) if \(\mat A^\T = -\mat A\), that is, \(A_{\mathrm{ij}} = -A_{\mathrm{ji}}\) for all \(i\) and \(j\).
