For a square matrix \(\mat A\) the matrix \(\tfrac12(\mat A + \mat A^\T)\) is its symmetric part (simetrični del) and the matrix \(\tfrac12(\mat A - \mat A^\T)\) its antisymmetric part (antisimetrični del).

Source: KREYSZIG §7.2, (11) (PDF p. 294), CM §2.3.4 (PDF p. 62).

So a symmetric matrix equals its mirror image across the main diagonal, while in an antisymmetric one the mirror image of every entry has the opposite sign. KREYSZIG calls an antisymmetric matrix skew-symmetric (KREYSZIG §7.2, PDF p. 294). The matrix \(\mat K\) of the cube is neither symmetric nor antisymmetric: the entry \(0{,}001\) in row \(x\) and column \(z\) has the mirror image \(0\), which is neither \(0{,}001\) nor \(-0{,}001\). The matrix \(\mat V\) of the hanging bar is neither one nor the other either. Its pair off the diagonal is antisymmetric, but the entries on the main diagonal are not zero, which an antisymmetric matrix does not allow, as we will show in the next lemma. Every square matrix, however, can be written as the sum of a symmetric and an antisymmetric one.

Lemma 1.103 Split into symmetric and antisymmetric parts (razcep na simetrični in antisimetrični del)

For every square matrix \(\mat A\):

  1. its symmetric part \(\tfrac12(\mat A + \mat A^\T)\) is a symmetric matrix, its antisymmetric part \(\tfrac12(\mat A - \mat A^\T)\) is an antisymmetric matrix, and their sum is \(\mat A\):
    \[\mat A = \tfrac12\,(\mat A + \mat A^\T) + \tfrac12\,(\mat A - \mat A^\T) , \tag{1.42}\]
  2. the split is unique: if \(\mat A = \mat B + \mat C\), where \(\mat B\) is a symmetric and \(\mat C\) an antisymmetric matrix, then \(\mat B = \tfrac12(\mat A + \mat A^\T)\) and \(\mat C = \tfrac12(\mat A - \mat A^\T)\),
  3. the entries on the main diagonal of an antisymmetric matrix are zero.
Proof

We must show three items. We use the rules of matrix arithmetic (lemma 1.95) and the rules for transposition (lemma 1.101).

1. The split.

  1. By item 2 of lemma 1.101, \(\big(\tfrac12(\mat A + \mat A^\T)\big)^\T = \tfrac12\big(\mat A^\T + (\mat A^\T)^\T\big)\).
  2. By item 1 of the same lemma, \((\mat A^\T)^\T = \mat A\), and by rule 1 of lemma 1.95, \(\mat A^\T + \mat A = \mat A + \mat A^\T\). So the symmetric part equals its transposed matrix and is symmetric.
  3. In the same way, \(\big(\tfrac12(\mat A - \mat A^\T)\big)^\T = \tfrac12\,(\mat A^\T - \mat A)\), where we transpose the difference as the sum \(\mat A + (-1)\,\mat A^\T\) by item 2 of lemma 1.101.
  4. The matrix \(\mat A^\T - \mat A\) has the entries \(A_{\mathrm{ji}} - A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), which are the opposites of the entries \(A_{\mathrm{ij}} - A_{\mathrm{ji}}\) of the matrix \(\mat A - \mat A^\T\) (definition 1.94). So \(\tfrac12\,(\mat A^\T - \mat A) = -\tfrac12\,(\mat A - \mat A^\T)\), and the antisymmetric part is antisymmetric.
  5. By rules 4 and 5 of lemma 1.95 the sum of the two parts is \(\tfrac12\mat A + \tfrac12\mat A^\T + \tfrac12\mat A - \tfrac12\mat A^\T = (\tfrac12 + \tfrac12)\,\mat A + (\tfrac12 - \tfrac12)\,\mat A^\T = \mat A\).

2. Uniqueness.

  1. Let \(\mat A = \mat B + \mat C\), where \(\mat B^\T = \mat B\) and \(\mat C^\T = -\mat C\).
  2. We transpose the equation. By item 2 of lemma 1.101, \(\mat A^\T = \mat B^\T + \mat C^\T = \mat B - \mat C\). This gives a second equation for the matrices \(\mat B\) and \(\mat C\).
  3. We add the two equations. The matrices \(\mat C\) and \(-\mat C\) cancel, and \(\mat A + \mat A^\T = 2\,\mat B\) remains. Multiplying by \(\tfrac12\) gives \(\mat B = \tfrac12(\mat A + \mat A^\T)\).
  4. We subtract the second equation from the first. What remains is \(\mat A - \mat A^\T = 2\,\mat C\), and after multiplying by \(\tfrac12\), \(\mat C = \tfrac12(\mat A - \mat A^\T)\).

3. The main diagonal of an antisymmetric matrix.

  1. Let \(\mat C\) be antisymmetric. By definition 1.102, \(C_{\mathrm{ij}} = -C_{\mathrm{ji}}\) for all \(i\) and \(j\), so also for \(j = i\): \(C_{\mathrm{ii}} = -C_{\mathrm{ii}}\).
  2. We add \(C_{\mathrm{ii}}\) to both sides and get \(2\,C_{\mathrm{ii}} = 0\), so \(C_{\mathrm{ii}} = 0\).

Source: CM (2.3.3) and §2.3.4 (PDF p. 62), KREYSZIG §7.2, (11) (PDF p. 294). The proof of uniqueness is not from a source.

The uniqueness of the split is shown by figure 1.333 on the same numbers as figure 1.332.

Let us draw the rows. The first is the split \(\mat A = \mat B + \mat C\), where \(\mat B\) is symmetric and \(\mat C\) antisymmetric. The second is the same split, transposed: \(\mat B\) stays, \(\mat C\) changes sign, because \(\mat C^\T = -\mat C\). The third adds the equations, \(\mat C\) cancels and \(2\,\mat B\) remains. The fourth subtracts the equations, \(\mat B\) cancels and \(2\,\mat C\) remains.

The split into parts is like writing a number as a sum, only here the two parts are determined: the symmetric part is the average of the matrix and its mirror image, the antisymmetric part half of their difference. The entry of the symmetric part in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is \(\tfrac12(A_{\mathrm{ij}} + A_{\mathrm{ji}})\), the entry of the antisymmetric part \(\tfrac12(A_{\mathrm{ij}} - A_{\mathrm{ji}})\).

For the hanging bar at the point \(P\), the symmetric part of the matrix \(\mat V\) is just its main diagonal, since the two entries of the pair, \(\mp 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}\), cancel in the average, and the zeros stay zeros. The antisymmetric part is the pair itself:

\[\begin{aligned} \mat V &= \begin{bmatrix} 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} \\ &\quad + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} & 0 \\ 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} . \end{aligned}\]

Let us draw the split. On the left is the matrix \(\mat V\), all entries in units of \(10^{-10}\), and in blue the pair off the main diagonal. The sign \(=\) equates it with the sum of two parts, joined by the sign \(+\). The symmetric part has the same main diagonal and zeros everywhere else. The antisymmetric part has the same pair and zeros on the main diagonal.

This is exactly what we learned about the bar in section 1.7.2. The symmetric part describes the stretching along the bar and the thinning across it, the antisymmetric part a small turn of the material close to the point \(P\) without shear.

For the cube the split is more instructive, because there the same shear splits into two parts that we can draw. By (1.42),

\[\mat K = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}0005 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0{,}0005 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}0005 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -0{,}0005 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

Let us draw the left half, the symmetric part. The axes in the corner show \(x\) to the right and \(z\) up. The blackwhite square is the front face of the cube before loading, the letters are its corners, and the label under it says which part of the matrix \(\mat K\) we are drawing. The orange quadrilateral is the face after this part. The ratio \(0{,}001\) is strongly enlarged so that the movements can be seen. The blue dimension line at \(B\) shows that \(B\) moves up. The blue dimension line above \(D\) shows that \(D\) moves to the right. Both dimension lines are set off from the edge with two grey auxiliary lines, so that they do not lie on the edge. The blue arrow at \(C\) is the sum of the two movements, obliquely up and to the right. So the edge \(AB\) tilts up, the edge \(AD\) to the right, that is towards each other, the diagonal \(AC\) gets longer and the diagonal \(BD\) shorter.

The sign \(+\) says that we add the middle half, the antisymmetric part. The square and the corners are the same, the label under them is different. The orange quadrilateral is the face after this part. The dimension line at \(B\) now points down, the dimension line above \(D\) again to the right, the arrow at \(C\) down and to the right. The right edge therefore goes down, the top edge to the right, and the face turns clockwise.

The sign \(=\) leads to the right half, the sum of both parts. The square, the corners and the label \(\mat K\) are the same as before. At \(B\) there is no dimension line, because the movement up from the symmetric part and the movement down from the antisymmetric part cancel, so \(B\) stays in place. The dimension line above \(D\) and the dimension line above \(C\) are equally long and horizontal, because the vertical parts cancel and the horizontal ones add. The orange parallelogram is the shear of the cube, in which the edge \(AB\) stays in place.

What does each part do to the front face \(ABCD\) of the cube (figure 1.335)? The corners are the same as in section 1.16.2 (figure 1.319), and we multiply each part by the vectors of the edges and diagonals from \(A\). The table collects all the products, the vectors are in micrometres, and so are the results:

vector symmetric part antisymmetric part sum, \(\mat K\)
\(\overrightarrow{AB} = (10\,000, 0, 0)\) \((0, 0, 5)\) \((0, 0, -5)\) \((0, 0, 0)\)
\(\overrightarrow{AD} = (0, 0, 10\,000)\) \((5, 0, 0)\) \((5, 0, 0)\) \((10, 0, 0)\)
\(\overrightarrow{AC} = (10\,000, 0, 10\,000)\) \((5, 0, 5)\) \((5, 0, -5)\) \((10, 0, 0)\)
\(\overrightarrow{BD} = (-10\,000, 0, 10\,000)\) \((5, 0, -5)\) \((5, 0, 5)\) \((10, 0, 0)\)

Let us take the rows apart.

  1. The symmetric part moves the end of the edge \(AB\) by \((0, 0, 5)\), upward, and the end of the edge \(AD\) by \((5, 0, 0)\), to the right. Each edge tilts toward the other by five ten-thousandths of its length, and the right angle at \(A\) closes equally from both sides. It moves the end of the diagonal \(AC\) by \((5, 0, 5)\), which is \(0{,}0005\) times the vector \((10\,000, 0, 10\,000)\): the diagonal lengthens by five ten-thousandths. The vector of the diagonal \(BD\), \((-10\,000, 0, 10\,000)\), gives \((5, 0, -5)\), which is \(-0{,}0005\) times this vector: the diagonal shortens by five ten-thousandths.
  2. The antisymmetric part moves the end of the edge \(AB\) by \((0, 0, -5)\), downward, and the end of the edge \(AD\) by \((5, 0, 0)\), to the right. Both edges tilt by five ten-thousandths of their length in the same direction, clockwise when we look at the face with the axis \(x\) to the right and the axis \(z\) up, as if the face were turned. The end of the diagonal \(AC\) moves by \((5, 0, -5)\), in the direction of the other diagonal, which is perpendicular to \(AC\), because the diagonals of a square are perpendicular. So the diagonal turns, but it does not lengthen.
  3. The sum of the two displacements is the displacement due to the matrix \(\mat K\). The end of the edge \(AB\) moves by \((0, 0, 5) + (0, 0, -5) = (0, 0, 0)\), the end of the edge \(AD\) by \((5, 0, 0) + (5, 0, 0) = (10, 0, 0)\). This is the shear of section 1.6.2.

So the shear of the cube is a stretching along one diagonal and a shortening along the other, to which a small turn of the whole face is added. How exactly is the antisymmetric part a turn? A true turn does not change lengths at all. The edge \(AB\), however, becomes \((10\,000, 0, 0) + (0, 0, -5) = (10\,000, 0, -5)\) under the antisymmetric part, with the length \(\sqrt{10\,000^2 + 5^2} = 10\,000{,}00125\) µm, which is \(1{,}25 \cdot 10^{-7}\) of the length more. This is the square of the number \(0{,}0005\) divided by \(2\), a term of the same kind as the strain \(5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) of the edge \(AD\) in section 1.6.2, which was the square of the ratio \(0{,}001\) divided by \(2\) and grew with the square of the push. So the antisymmetric part is a turn only up to such negligible terms. Why this matters, the corollary below says: the antisymmetric part does not change the length of a fibre.

The double sum (1.41) with the same column on both sides has one more property, which we will need in section 1.17.

Corollary 1.104 The double sum and the antisymmetric part (dvojna vsota in antisimetrični del)

Let \(\vek v\) be a column with \(n\) entries. Then:

  1. for every antisymmetric matrix \(\mat C\) of order \(n\), \(\vek v^\T\mat C\vek v = 0\),
  2. for every square matrix \(\mat A\) of order \(n\), \(\vek v^\T\mat A\vek v = \vek v^\T \big(\tfrac12(\mat A + \mat A^\T)\big)\,\vek v\).
Proof

We must show that an antisymmetric matrix contributes nothing to the double sum, and that therefore only the symmetric part contributes.

1. An antisymmetric matrix.

  1. By (1.41), \(\vek v^\T\mat C\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{n} \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} v_{\mathrm{i}}\,C_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\), a sum of \(n^2\) terms, one for each pair of indices \((i, j)\).
  2. The terms with \(i = j\) are zero, because by item 3 of lemma 1.103 the entries \(C_{\mathrm{ii}}\) on the main diagonal of an antisymmetric matrix are zero.
  3. We divide the terms with \(i \neq j\) into pairs: the term for the pair \((i, j)\) and the term for the pair \((j, i)\). The sum of the two is \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\,C_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}} + v_{\mathrm{j}}\,C_{\mathrm{ji}}\,v_{\mathrm{i}} = v_{\mathrm{i}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\,(C_{\mathrm{ij}} + C_{\mathrm{ji}})\), after we rearrange the factors and take out \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  4. The matrix \(\mat C\) is antisymmetric, so \(C_{\mathrm{ji}} = -C_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (definition 1.102), and the sum of each pair is zero.
  5. Every term is either zero or in a pair whose sum is zero, so the whole sum is zero.

2. The symmetric part.

  1. By item 1 of lemma 1.103, \(\mat A = \mat B + \mat C\), where \(\mat B = \tfrac12(\mat A + \mat A^\T)\) is symmetric and \(\mat C = \tfrac12(\mat A - \mat A^\T)\) antisymmetric.
  2. By item 3 of lemma 1.99, used twice, \(\vek v^\T\,(\mat B + \mat C)\,\vek v = \vek v^\T\mat B\vek v + \vek v^\T\mat C\vek v\).
  3. By item 1, \(\vek v^\T\mat C\vek v = 0\), so \(\vek v^\T\mat A\vek v = \vek v^\T\mat B\vek v\).

Source: KREYSZIG §8.4, (7) and Example 5 (PDF p. 369) says that in the double sum \(\vek v^\T\mat A\vek v\) the matrix may be replaced by a symmetric one. The proof is not from a source.

We test item 1 on numbers (figure 1.336).

Let us draw this. The vector \(\vek v = (1, 2, 3)\) is the column we calculate with. The matrix \(\mat C\) is antisymmetric: entries that stand as mirror images across the main diagonal have opposite signs, and each pair has its own colour. The main diagonal is zero. On the right are nine terms, the expression \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\,C_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\) above them says how they are built, in the same arrangement as the entries of the matrix. The diagonal terms are zero. The terms of each mirror pair have the same colour and are opposite, for example \(4\) and \(-4\), because \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\) stays while the entry \(C_{\mathrm{ij}}\) changes sign. The sum of each pair is therefore zero, and so is the sum of all terms.

Books call the expression \(\vek v^\T\mat A\vek v\) a quadratic form (kvadratna forma) (KREYSZIG §8.4, (7), PDF p. 369), because each of its terms is a product of two components of the vector, but we do not need the name in what follows. Let us try the corollary on the cube. Take the unit vector in the direction of the diagonal \(AC\), \(\vek n = (1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\), whose length is \(\sqrt{1/2 + 0 + 1/2} = 1\). In the double sum with the matrix \(\mat K\) only the term with the entry \(K_{\mathrm{xz}}\) is nonzero:

\[\vek n^\T\mat K\vek n = n_{\mathrm{x}}\,K_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} \cdot 0{,}001 \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt2} = 0{,}0005 .\]

The symmetric part has the entries \(0{,}0005\) in row \(x\) and column \(z\) and in row \(z\) and column \(x\), so the double sum with it has two terms:

\[\vek n^\T\,\tfrac12(\mat K + \mat K^\T)\,\vek n = n_{\mathrm{x}} \cdot 0{,}0005 \cdot n_{\mathrm{z}} + n_{\mathrm{z}} \cdot 0{,}0005 \cdot n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}00025 + 0{,}00025 = 0{,}0005 .\]

The antisymmetric part has the entries \(0{,}0005\) and \(-0{,}0005\), and the terms are \(0{,}00025\) and \(-0{,}00025\), which cancel to \(0\). For the direction of the diagonal \(BD\), \(\vek n = (-1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\), we get \(-0{,}0005\). These are the strains of the diagonals of section 1.6.2, \(+5{,}001 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and \(-4{,}999 \cdot 10^{-4}\), up to the small terms with the square of the push. The agreement is no coincidence. In section 1.17 we will show that the strain of a short fibre in the direction of a unit vector \(\vek n\) is approximately such a double sum with the matrix of partial derivatives. The corollary tells why the turn does not count there: the antisymmetric part moves the end of a fibre across it, as for the diagonal \(AC\) above, so it turns the fibre but does not lengthen it.

Books write matrices in different ways. CM writes a matrix in square brackets, \([A]\), and its entries with a small letter, \(a_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (CM §2.3.1, PDF p. 60), while KREYSZIG writes it with a bold letter \(\mathbf A\) and its entries as \(a_{\mathrm{jk}}\) (KREYSZIG §7.1, PDF p. 284). SADD writes the matrix of partial derivatives of the displacement as \(u_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}}\), where a comma in the index means the partial derivative with respect to the variable with the index \(j\) (SADD (2.1.4), (2.1.5), PDF p. 40), and CM with the sign \(\nabla\) and a transposition (CM (3.3.8), PDF p. 120). We will write \(\mat A\) and \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and partial derivatives always with the sign \(\partial\).

1.16.5 The identity matrix and the inverse matrix

For the sheared cube, whose matrix \(\mat K\) has the only nonzero entry \(0{,}001\) in row \(x\) and column \(z\), we wrote the vector of a fibre after loading as \(\vek v + \mat K\vek v\). We would like to write it as a single product with a matrix, just as in section 1.16.3 we wrote the vector with the components \(v_{\mathrm{x}} + 0{,}001\,v_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\). For this we need a matrix that leaves the vector \(\vek v\) unchanged, and we add it to the matrix \(\mat K\). Figure 1.337 shows what it looks like.

Let us draw it. The identity matrix \(\mat I\) is a \(3 \times 3\) table. The ones are blue and lie on the main diagonal, all other entries are zero. Above the columns are written the unit vectors of the axes \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), because each column of the matrix \(\mat I\) is exactly this vector: column \(x\) is \((1, 0, 0)\). On the right we multiply it by the column \(\vek v\). The sign \(=\) leads to the result \(\mat I\vek v\). Let us look at its entry \(x\). Marked in blue are row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat I\), \((1, 0, 0)\), and the entry \(x\) of the result. The row \((1, 0, 0)\) multiplies \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) by \(1\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) by \(0\) and \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) by \(0\), so it gives only \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\). Likewise rows \(y\) and \(z\) give \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\). The result is therefore the same column \(\vek v\).

Definition 1.105 Identity matrix (enotska matrika)

The identity matrix of order \(n\), \(\mat I\) (enotska matrika), is the square matrix of order \(n\) that has ones on the main diagonal, while all other entries are zero:

\[I_{\mathrm{ij}} = 1 \ \text{for}\ i = j , \qquad I_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0 \ \text{for}\ i \neq j .\]

For \(n = 3\) it is

\[\mat I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

Source: KREYSZIG §7.2 (PDF p. 294), CM §2.3.1 (PDF p. 60).

The columns of the identity matrix of order \(3\) are the unit vectors of the axes \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) ((1.12)), written vertically. When the order matters we write it as an index, \(\mat I_{\mathrm{n}}\), otherwise we read it off the matrices that we add to \(\mat I\) or multiply by it.

Lemma 1.106 Multiplication by the identity matrix (množenje z enotsko matriko)

For every column \(\vek v\) with \(n\) entries, \(\mat I_{\mathrm{n}}\,\vek v = \vek v\). For every matrix \(\mat A\) of size \(m \times n\), \(\mat I_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mat A = \mat A\) and \(\mat A\,\mat I_{\mathrm{n}} = \mat A\).

Proof

We must show that the two sides of each equality agree in all entries.

  1. By (1.38) the entry \(i\) of the column \(\mat I_{\mathrm{n}}\,\vek v\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} I_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  2. By definition 1.105, \(I_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) in this sum for every \(j \neq i\), so all terms except the term with \(j = i\) are zero. That term is \(I_{\mathrm{ii}}\,v_{\mathrm{i}} = 1 \cdot v_{\mathrm{i}} = v_{\mathrm{i}}\). So the entry \(i\) of the column \(\mat I_{\mathrm{n}}\,\vek v\) is \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\), and \(\mat I_{\mathrm{n}}\,\vek v = \vek v\).
  3. By (1.40) the entry \((i, k)\) of the matrix \(\mat I_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mat A\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{m} I_{\mathrm{ij}}\,A_{\mathrm{jk}}\). As in step 2, only the term with \(j = i\) remains, which is \(A_{\mathrm{ik}}\).
  4. The entry \((i, k)\) of the matrix \(\mat A\,\mat I_{\mathrm{n}}\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,I_{\mathrm{jk}}\). Only the term with \(j = k\) remains, which is \(A_{\mathrm{ik}} \cdot 1 = A_{\mathrm{ik}}\).

Source: KREYSZIG §7.2, (13) (PDF p. 294), CM §2.3.5, remark (8) (PDF p. 64).

Let us draw the top row. The axes on the left show \(x\) to the right and \(z\) up. The blackwhite square is the front face of the cube before loading, and the blue arrow is the vector of its vertical edge \(AD\). The arrow \(\mat I + \mat K\) means that we multiply every fibre vector by \(\mat I + \mat K\). The orange parallelogram is the face after loading, and the top edge is shifted to the right. The shift is strongly enlarged, in reality the ratio is \(0{,}001\). The blue arrow is the vector of the edge after loading, tilted to the right. The arrow \(\mat I - \mat K\) means the opposite way. The blackwhite square and the blue arrow are again as at the start, the fibres are returned to their position before loading.

In the multiplication of matrices the identity matrix plays the role that the number \(1\) plays in the multiplication of numbers. For the cube we now have \(\vek v + \mat K\vek v = \mat I\vek v + \mat K\vek v = (\mat I + \mat K)\,\vek v\), by lemma 1.106 and item 3 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product, used for the column \(\vek v\). The matrix

\[\mat I + \mat K = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0{,}001 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

is exactly the matrix we guessed at the beginning of section 1.16.3. It sends the vector of every fibre before loading to its vector after loading (figure 1.338, top). For the edge \(AD\), \((\mat I + \mat K)\,(0, 0, 10\,000) = (10, 0, 10\,000)\).

Can we reverse the way and compute the vector of a fibre before loading from its vector after loading? For the cube the answer is simple: we push the top face back by 10 µm. This rule subtracts \(0{,}001\) times the component \(z\) from the component \(x\). We guess that its matrix is \(\mat I - \mat K\), and we check it. For the edge \(AD\) the component \(x\) of the product \((\mat I - \mat K)\,(10, 0, 10\,000)\) is \(10 - 0{,}001 \cdot 10\,000 = 0\), and the other two components are \(0\) and \(10\,000\). So the product is \((0, 0, 10\,000)\), the edge before loading. Let us check that this holds for every fibre by computing the product of the two matrices.

  1. By item 3 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product, \((\mat I - \mat K)(\mat I + \mat K) = \mat I\mat I + \mat I\mat K - \mat K\mat I - \mat K\mat K\).
  2. By lemma 1.106, \(\mat I\mat I = \mat I\), \(\mat I\mat K = \mat K\) and \(\mat K\mat I = \mat K\), so the two middle terms cancel, and \(\mat I - \mat K\mat K\) remains.
  3. The entry \((i, k)\) of the product \(\mat K\mat K\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} K_{\mathrm{ij}}\,K_{\mathrm{jk}}\) ((1.40)). Only a term with \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} \neq 0\) could be nonzero, that is, a term with \(i = x\) and \(j = z\). That term is \(K_{\mathrm{xz}}\,K_{\mathrm{zk}}\), and \(K_{\mathrm{zk}} = 0\) for every \(k\), because row \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat K\) is zero. So \(\mat K\mat K = \mat 0\).
  4. Therefore \((\mat I - \mat K)(\mat I + \mat K) = \mat I\). In the same way \((\mat I + \mat K)(\mat I - \mat K) = \mat I + \mat K - \mat K - \mat K\mat K = \mat I\).

Step 3 is shown by figure 1.339.

Let us draw this. The matrix \(\mat K\) has a single nonzero entry, \(0{,}001\), in blue in the row \(x\) and column \(z\). The shaded row \(z\) is zero. The vector \(\vek v\) in the \(x\)-\(z\) plane has a component \(z\) that is grey dashed. The first arrow \(\mat K\) sends it to the horizontal vector \(\mat K\vek v\): the component \(x\) becomes \(0{,}001\,v_{\mathrm{z}}\), the other two are zero. The second arrow \(\mat K\) acts on a horizontal vector, which has no component \(z\), so the result is the zero vector.

So the matrix \(\mat I - \mat K\) undoes the action of the matrix \(\mat I + \mat K\), in both orders (figure 1.338, top).

By the way, \(\mat K\mat K = \mat 0\) although \(\mat K\) is not the zero matrix. With numbers nothing like this happens, with matrices it does. A matrix that undoes another, as \(\mat I - \mat K\) does for \(\mat I + \mat K\), gets a name.

Definition 1.107 Inverse matrix (inverzna matrika)

Let \(\mat A\) be a square matrix of order \(n\). A square matrix \(\mat B\) of order \(n\) for which

\[\mat A\mat B = \mat B\mat A = \mat I \tag{1.43}\]

is an inverse matrix (inverzna matrika) of the matrix \(\mat A\). A matrix that has an inverse matrix is invertible (obrnljiva).

Source: KREYSZIG §7.8, (1) (PDF p. 327), CM §2.3.6 (PDF p. 65).

The definition asks for both equalities, \(\mat A\mat B = \mat I\) and \(\mat B\mat A = \mat I\), because the matrix product is not commutative (item 4 of lemma 1.99), and we do not know in advance that one follows from the other. By the calculation above, the matrix \(\mat I - \mat K\) is the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat I + \mat K\). The name invertible says that the action of such a matrix can be reversed: from \(\mat A\vek v\) we get \(\vek v\) back, since by item 1 of lemma 1.99 and lemma 1.106 \(\mat B\,(\mat A\vek v) = (\mat B\mat A)\,\vek v = \mat I\vek v = \vek v\). Books also call an invertible matrix nonsingular (nesingularna), and a matrix without an inverse singular (singularna) (KREYSZIG §7.8, PDF p. 327). We define the inverse matrix only for square matrices, as both sources do (KREYSZIG §7.8, PDF p. 327, CM §2.3.6, PDF p. 65). Can a matrix have two different inverse matrices? It cannot.

Lemma 1.108 Uniqueness of the inverse matrix (enoličnost inverzne matrike)

If \(\mat B\) and \(\mat C\) are inverse matrices of a square matrix \(\mat A\), then \(\mat B = \mat C\).

Proof

We must show that \(\mat B\) and \(\mat C\) are equal. We turn the matrix \(\mat B\) into \(\mat C\) by a chain of equalities.

  1. By lemma 1.106, \(\mat B = \mat B\,\mat I\).
  2. The matrix \(\mat C\) is an inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat A\), so \(\mat A\mat C = \mat I\) ((1.43)), and \(\mat B = \mat B\,(\mat A\mat C)\).
  3. By item 2 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product, \(\mat B\,(\mat A\mat C) = (\mat B\mat A)\,\mat C\).
  4. The matrix \(\mat B\) is an inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat A\), so \(\mat B\mat A = \mat I\), and \((\mat B\mat A)\,\mat C = \mat I\,\mat C = \mat C\) by lemma 1.106.
  5. Steps 1 to 4 give \(\mat B = \mat C\).

Source: CM §2.3.6 (PDF p. 65), KREYSZIG §7.8 (PDF p. 327).

The uniqueness is shown by figure 1.340 on the cube.

Let us draw this. The axes \(x\) and \(z\) define the plane. The vector \(\vek u\) points upwards. The matrix \(\mat A = \mat I + \mat K\) sends it to the vector \(\vek w = \mat A\vek u\), tilted to the right. The orange arc is the inverse matrix \(\mat C\), which returns the tip of the vector \(\vek w\) to the tip of the vector \(\vek u\). The blue arc is the other inverse matrix \(\mat B\). The proof shows that it returns the tip of the vector \(\vek w\) to the same point as \(\mat C\).

Since the inverse matrix is unique, we may denote it by a single symbol, \(\mat A^{-1}\). For the cube, \((\mat I + \mat K)^{-1} = \mat I - \mat K\). The proof used only the grouping of factors and the identity matrix, nothing else.

Does every square matrix have an inverse matrix? No. Take the matrix

\[\mat N = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

for which \(\mat N\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\). It pushes every vector into the horizontal plane \(z = 0\), as if we pressed a piece of material into a plate with no thickness. Let us show that \(\mat N\) is not invertible.

  1. Suppose that \(\mat B\) is a matrix of order \(3\) with \(\mat B\mat N = \mat I\).
  2. By (1.38), \(\mat N\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 0, 0)\). Row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat N\), \((1, 0, 0)\), times the column \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 0, 1)\) gives \(0\), and so does row \(y\), \((0, 1, 0)\), while row \(z\) is zero.
  3. By item 1 of lemma 1.99 therefore \((\mat B\mat N)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \mat B\,(\mat N\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = \mat B\,\vek 0\), and every entry of the product \(\mat B\,\vek 0\) is a sum of products with zero, so zero.
  4. By assumption and lemma 1.106, however, \((\mat B\mat N)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \mat I\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 0, 1)\), which is not the zero vector. This contradicts step 3.
  5. So there is no matrix \(\mat B\) with \(\mat B\mat N = \mat I\), and \(\mat N\) has no inverse matrix.

The proof is shown by figure 1.341.

Let us draw this. The blue arrow is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The matrix \(\mat N\) sends it to the zero vector, a point at the origin. The matrix \(\mat B\) sends the zero vector again to the zero vector, because every entry of the product \(\mat B\,\vek 0\) is a sum of products with zero. If \(\mat B\mat N = \mat I\) held, the image of the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) would have to be the grey dashed arrow, and that is not the zero vector.

Let us also draw the bottom row of figure 1.338. The blackwhite square is again the face before the mapping. The blue arrow \(\vek a\) is its bottom edge and the blue arrow \(\vek b\) the diagonal, both from the bottom left corner. The square is drawn on a larger scale than in the text, where \(\vek a = (1, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek b = (1, 0, 1)\). The arrow \(\mat N\) means multiplication by \(\mat N\). The grey line is the plane \(z = 0\), seen from the front, and the orange segment on it is the square after the mapping, since \(\mat N\) takes the height away from every point. The blue arrow above the segment is the result for both vectors at once, \(\mat N\vek a = \mat N\vek b\). It is drawn slightly above the segment so that it does not overlap with it.

Why it fails is shown by this row of the figure. The matrix \(\mat N\) sends the different vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) to the same vector \((1, 0, 0)\). From the result we therefore cannot tell which vector it came from, and no rule can bring it back. Invertibility means that from a fibre after loading we can get the fibre before loading again, as for the cube with the matrix \(\mat I - \mat K\). In the deformation of a body this does not happen. A fibre that has a positive length before loading cannot have the length zero after loading, because that is physically impossible, and CM concludes from this that the matrices which send the vector of every fibre before loading to its vector after loading are invertible (CM §3.3.1, PDF pp. 119-120). That a matrix which sends no nonzero vector to the zero vector really has an inverse matrix, and how to compute that inverse matrix, we will show in chapter 2. There we will compute from the entries of a square matrix of order \(3\) a single number that tells whether the matrix is invertible.

Let us sum up how we arrived at these tools. We wrote the nine partial derivatives of (1.36) as a matrix and the three sums as the product of the matrix and the column of the step, and got the single equation (1.39). On the cube we saw that one entry, \(0{,}001\), of the matrix \(\mat K\) carries the whole deformation, and that the vector of every fibre after loading is the matrix \(\mat I + \mat K\) times its vector before loading. On the bar, the product \(\mat V\vek n\) gave us in one calculation all three components of the difference of displacements of a fibre per unit length. We derived the product of two matrices from two rules one after the other and saw that the order matters. The split into symmetric and antisymmetric parts divided the shear of the cube into a stretching along the diagonals and a turn, and the double sum does not see the antisymmetric part. In the next section we will use these tools to compute the strain of a short fibre in any direction for every continuously differentiable displacement field. The vector that a short fibre has after loading will be approximately the product of the matrix of partial derivatives plus the identity matrix and the vector before loading. We will write the square of its length with transposition, and the split into symmetric and antisymmetric parts will separate the stretching of the material from its turning.
